pending_news.title: Рождественский ЕР от ICE NINE KILLS
pending_news.rss_body:
ICE NINE KILLS девятого ноября в цифровом варианте выпустят новый ЕР "A Very Vicious Christmas", в который войдут интерпретации рождественской классики, записанные для "Terror Tram Starring Art The Clown" в Universal Studios Hollywood.

Spencer Charnas: «Это наш ранний подарок на Рождество. Когда нам поручили создать музыкальное сопровождение к нападению Арта Клоуна на «Трамвай ужаса», мы сразу поняли суть задания. Арт обожает Рождество. А кто, как не ICE NINE KILLS, сможет так безвкусно разделаться с некоторыми рождественскими классическими песнями?

С такими текстами, как „О, как же весело умереть в открытом катафалке“ и „Он измельчит твои конечности, как колбасный фарш“, мы не были уверены, что найдём детский хор, родители которого одобрили бы такое, но, к счастью, дух праздника возобладал.

Для нас большая честь, что сценарист и режиссёр «Terrifier» Damien Leone, продюсер Phil Falcone и их команда пригласили нас в свою кровавую песочницу.

«Halloween Horror Nights» — одно из наших любимых мест, и в этом году оно обещает быть ещё более праздничным».

pending_news.title: Гитарист TYPE O NEGATIVE: «Благодаря TikTok мы сейчас очень известны»
pending_news.rss_body:
В недавнем интервью Kenny Hickey поговорил о своем пребывании в составе TYPE O NEGATIVE. Коллектив, по сути, прекратил существование после смерти фронтмена Питера Стила: в апреле 2010 года он скончался от сердечной недостаточности в возрасте 48 лет.

«Если оглянуться назад, я считаю, всё в TYPE O должно было сложиться именно так, как сложилось, — сказал гитарист. — Улучшить можно что угодно, но исторически это уже стало самостоятельным явлением.

И никто не захочет ничего менять. Я бы и сам сейчас ничего не стал менять».

TYPE O NEGATIVE сформировались в конце 1980-х, после распада прежней группы Стила, CARNIVORE. Коллектив просуществовал двадцать лет и обзавёлся мощной армией поклонников благодаря частым гастролям и семи студийным альбомам.

Что до того, как сегодня музыку TYPE O воспринимают любители хард-рока и хеви-металла, Kenny сказал:

«Команда популярна как никогда. Как никогда! Моей младшей дочери сейчас 24. Я приезжал к ней в колледж, и вокруг были сплошные фанаты TYPE O. Так что мы дотянулись до совершенно нового поколения…

Наше первое поколение слушателей, по большей части, ещё живо, а теперь к нему добавились ещё два. Так что дела идут лучше некуда, дружище».

Рост популярности TYPE O NEGATIVE в последние годы Hickey проиллюстрировал так:

«Мы только что получили золотой сертификат за стриминг. Знаешь, сколько прослушиваний для этого нужно? 250 миллионов! Столько набрал сингл "I Don't Wanna Be Me". Он выстрелил в TikTok, и это буквально взорвало интерес к группе, а теперь вся остальная наша музыка открылась этим ребятам. Вот что происходит. Благослови Бог TikTok. Благослови Бог TikTok!»

И добавил:

«Посмотри, что TikTok сделал с CROWBAR. Тяжелейший дум-коллектив, у которого вообще не было коммерческого потенциала, сегодня собирает 1,9 миллиона слушателей на Spotify. Они взлетают по всему миру, и всё благодаря тому, что... Такое могло случиться только в TikTok. Их открыли эти ребята».

На вопрос, возможно ли, что он объединится с оставшимися в живых участниками TYPE O NEGATIVE ради концерта памяти Стила с приглашёнными музыкантами, Kenny ответил:

«С точки зрения логистики сейчас — нет, это невозможно. Но никогда не говори "никогда". Предложения есть. Просто не сейчас».

Ранее Kenny Hickey рассказывал, что бывший клавишник TYPE O NEGATIVE Josh Silver, женатый на сестре его жены, не готов брать на себя обязательства по трибьют-проекту в память о Стиле: он долгое время работал парамедиком в Нью-Йорке на городскую службу.

Кроме того, Kenny подтвердил, что полноформатная запись концерта давно распавшегося коллектива готовится к официальному выпуску.

pending_news.title: Track Premiere: Invulation – “Third Degree Warfare”
pending_news.rss_body:
I’m really excited to show everyone this song today. There’s a few styles of death metal that seem to endlessly endure over time, having been long-established as pillars of the sound’s brutal legacy. This includes the especially bestial variant on display with

Invulation

‘s new song, “Third Degree Warfare.” It’s a style that packs all the power of

Immolation

and

Formulas

-era

Morbid Angel

but is delivered with the blasphemous, iconoclastic attitude of bands like

Angelcorpse

,

Archgoat

and

Blaspherian

. There’s probably a bit of

Hate Eternal

and

Dead Congregation

in there as well.

But aside from these comparisons, here’s what you need to know: the song is a thrilling, well-composed composition of volcanic death metal. If you want to hear something that embodies sheer ferocity and power, it’s hard to beat a sound like this. Nothing needs to be innovated, reimagined, or reinvented here. All you need is dedication, good writing, and the right guitar tones.

Here’s what the project’s mastermind, Andrew Lampe, tells us about the song:

“Fire has always been a tool for inflicting maximum destruction and pain upon the enemy. Only the most diabolical will praise the inhumanity of war and the use of incendiary and chemical weapons on an entire population.”

Regarding the upcoming album, he sums it up with the cheerful thought that “”Humanity has brought its destruction upon itself through its endless desire for conquest and masochism — the culmination of our terminal illness bringing about a cleansing fire. The inferno now descends to burn away the mistakes of a people gone mad.”

Listen to “Third Degree Warfare” below (that song title goes hard, damn). And keep your ears set

for October 30 when

Inferno Descends

will unleash its full destructive fire upon us all.

pending_news.title: Roger Waters Presents Legacy: A Pink Floyd Show adds UK and Ireland dates
pending_news.rss_body:
The

Roger Waters

-sanctioned

Pink Floyd

tribute show Roger Waters Presents Legacy – A Pink Floyd Show will visit the UK and Ireland next year.

Roger Waters isn't part of the tour, but the 10-piece band will be directed by his son Harry Waters.

North American dates

for the production were announced last week.

The UK and Ireland shows commence on June 16 at Manchester O2 Apollo and run through to June 29 at Dublin's 3Arena.

"These songs have meant so much to so many people for so many years, and I’m excited for audiences to come together and experience them live again," says Roger Waters. "Harry has assembled a terrific band, and I can’t wait for fans around the world to see the special show we’ve created together."

"I fell in love with the music immediately," says Harry Waters. "It really had an impact on me, irrespective of any bias, because it was Dad’s music. I still love it deeply to this day. Collaborating with Dad on this new production is such an honour, and I’m so grateful to have the opportunity to bring this music to fans old and new, around the world."

Waters Jr.'s connections to the music of Pink Floyd run deep.

As a two-year-old, his voice was used on Pink Floyd’s

Goodbye Blue Sky

, and he played in his father's solo band for 14 years before being fired prior to the Us + Them tour in 2016.

pending_news.title: “Greg Lake said, ‘I can’t believe they played Schizoid Man like this”: Italian proggers’ trick got them a record deal
pending_news.rss_body:
In 2017 Italian prog legends

Premiata Forneria Marconi

signed to InsideOut and released bilingual album

Emotional Tattoos

. That year

Prog

visited the band in their Milan studios to discuss how they continued challenging themselves after nearly 50 years, what it was like being mentored by

Greg Lake

– and that time they ate spaghetti with

Jaco Pastorius

and

Joni Mitchell

.

In the wilfully obtuse world of prog, artists are not often known for doing things the easy way. But while some challenge themselves in terms of instrumental technique, performance or lyrical concepts, Italian prog pioneers Premiata Forneria Marconi set themselves a slightly more unusual task while making their new studio album – or, albums –

Emotional Tattoos

.

“This time we decided to do two different records,” explains singer and drummer Franz Di Cioccio. “The same music, but one in Italian and one in English. It’s the better way to understand what we want to sing about.”

“We made them together at the same time,” says bassist Patrick Djivas. “First the Italian then the English. Sometimes the two were racing each other to be finished.”

However, the lyrics on one album don’t necessarily correspond to the other. “How can you say exactly the same things to Italians or to Americans or British people?” asks Djivas. “Especially as Italy has a way of thinking that’s so different to the rest of the world.”

To demonstrate, the pair sit

Prog

down in their Milan studio and play the English album. The atmospheric 7/8 piano figure of

Morning Freedom (

renamed

Oniro

for the Italian version) rings from the speakers. When we come to the chorus after which the English version is named, Di Cioccio explains: “We had the English phrase for the chorus first: ‘

Moor-ning Freeee-dom’

. If we’d translated that directly into Italian, it would be

‘mat-i-no di li-ber-ta.’

It would be a completely different rhythm to the line and feel completely different, not reflecting the emotion it’s supposed to show.

“So in Italian it’s

‘sogni liberi’

–

‘make the dream free’

. From there we build a different lyric. It’s a difficult exercise, but we like it that way.”

Fans of the band since their acclaimed 70s output will be aware that making records in Italian and English is not new for PFM. But back when they made career-defining albums such as

Photos Of Ghosts

, they could rely on the services of one of prog’s most celebrated lyricists to bring their visions to life in a foreign tongue.

“We had Mr

Pete Sinfield

writing lyrics for us,” says Djivas. “He was really heavy on us until we sang it really good in English. But this time Franz did a good job – I think it sounds pretty natural.”

They continue to get their message across; and in both languages the themes are similar:

There’s A Fire In Me

and

It’s My Road

offer up the power of music as a force to heal in the face of a fractious world;

The Lesson

takes a “no pain, no gain” philosophy to the challenges of life and love; and opening track

We’re Not An Island

sounds remarkably apposite to anyone wondering what’s to become of the UK post-Brexit and the US post-Trump, even though Djivas and Di Cioccio insist they had less specific social sentiments to impart.

Most striking of all, though, both lyrically and musically, is

A Day We Share

, which surveys a global landscape in search of common ground, despite observing scenes such as: ‘

El Paso, Texas, almost in the middle of the night, watching the wall, waiting for the call to tear it all, another Berlin until we win

…’

The six-minute journey starts with rhythmic punches of acoustic guitar and florid keyboard swoops and swirls, before stepping up the drama with a mesmerising battery of staccato rock riffs; then it unexpectedly sidestepping into a more groove-based, almost rap-like section of stream-of-consciousness observation. Then the curtains are thrown open onto a big, anthemic chorus and a joyfully upbeat Celtic-tinged denouement. Reports of PFM mellowing with age have, it seems, been exaggerated. “We wouldn’t want to play like we did back then,” says Djivas. “It would bore us to death. But we still like to challenge ourselves.”

We were excited by the music from abroad. King Crimson, Jethro Tull, we got the feeling the wind was changing in our favour

Only the 71-year-old Di Cioccio remains from their founding line-up, which formed when a Milan‑based quartet of session musicians expanded to a five-piece in a bid to explore more adventurous musical avenues. Djivas would join their ranks a couple of years later on bass – but first, they had to establish themselves within a highly sceptical local industry.

“We were excited by the music we were hearing from abroad at that time,” says Di Cioccio. “

King Crimson

,

Jethro Tull

, Ekseption… we just got the feeling the wind was changing in our favour. So we changed our name and began to move to a more improvisational style. People couldn’t understand why we called ourselves Premiata Forneria Marconi – Award-Winning Bakery.

“When we played our first show under that name, the promoter wouldn’t even announce us! We were opening for

Deep Purple

, and support acts weren’t that common in Italy then. He thought if he announced a band that wasn’t Deep Purple, just a local band, everyone would throw things at us; and if he told them we were called Premiata Forneria Marconi they'd think, ‘What the hell is this?’ So he just refused to introduce us.”

He didn’t even tell the venue crew to turn the stage lights on – so as they stepped onto the stage in darkness, their only option, as the enduring cliché would have it, was to let their music do the talking. “Back then we used to play covers, like most bands do at first, so we began playing

21st Century Schizoid Man

,” says Di Cioccio. “We used to play the part where they stop and start – the really complicated bit – just looking at the ground and not at our instruments. It would make people a bit shocked that we could play it without looking. At the end the promoter sees the reaction for us, gets up on stage and says, ‘This is Premiata Forneria Marconi. You will be hearing a lot more about them!’”

He wasn’t wrong: over the coming months, numerous like‑minded compatriots would emerge with similarly avant-garde sounds, many of whom just happened to have curiously elongated names, such as Banco Del Mutuo Soccorso and Biglietto per l’inferno. The Italian prog scene was snowballing, and its leading lights were about to get a major break.

ELP had hired a mobile studio but they couldn’t record. Since they’d paid for it they said, ‘Do you want to record your show?

“Greg Lake was given a tape of us when

ELP

played in Italy. After a month he calls our manager Franco Mamone and he says, ‘Hey, I can’t believe these guys played that song [

Schizoid Man

] like this!’ He says, ‘I want to see them playing it. I used to play with King Crimson and I know how hard it is.’”

A London showcase gig was set up; and, duly impressed, Lake signed PFM to his new label Manticore. Their mentor, keen to introduce them to the English and American markets, hooked the quintet up with erstwhile Crimson lyricist Pete Sinfield. But Sinfield and Lake had a suggestion to make first. “They said, ‘English speakers can’t pronounce Premiata Forneria Marconi’ – they would always put the wrong emphasis on the syllables – Prem-eee-tur Forn-eerie-yur Marconi or something – people knew Marconi because it’s a famous name but otherwise people struggled with it. So we said, ‘We’ll just call ourselves PFM.’”

With Sinfield they set about turning songs from their second album,

Per un Amico

, into an English language release.

Photos Of Ghosts

was also beefed up with a reworked instrumental from their debut,

Storia di un Minuto

. The finished article juxtaposed dazzling, urgent bursts of jazz rock with pastoral, classically tinged folk rock, warped psychedelia and ebullient synth-heavy prog. Helped by

Celebration

becoming an FM radio hit,

Photos Of Ghosts

made them the first Italian act to enter the Billboard Top 200 album chart.

(Image credit: Courtesy of PFM)

By that time, Djivas had joined and the band were touring incessantly, thrilling crowds with improvisation-heavy shows of the kind that had made the

Grateful Dead

famous. And how better to capture that magic than with a live album? “ELP had hired a mobile studio in Central Park, but something happened and they couldn’t record that day,” says Di Cioccio. “Since they’d paid for it anyway, they said, ‘Do you want to record your show?’ We agreed – but we pretty much forgot about the recording, so we played normally, improvised pretty much the whole show, and that really made it so much better! Sometimes if you’re aware you’re being recorded live, you’re trying not to make mistakes, and it turns out a bit stiff.”

That recording formed part of

Cook

, a defining album for PFM, retitled and repackaged as

Live In The USA

for its European release. By that point, it felt like there had never been a better time to make music. The band had found a home from home just off LA’s Sunset Strip, on Alta Loma Road, as referenced in the extended jam

Alta Loma Five ’Till Nine,

which they created there.

The cover was an flag with chocolate inside, but the flag wrapper has been thrown away. We didn’t understand the weight of making fun of America

They would also stay at the Sunset Marquis hotel. “All the musicians stayed there,” Djivas recalls. “There was a party every night.”

Di Cioccio adds: “I remember one night when

Jaco Pastorius

was recording

Hejira

with

Joni Mitchell

. They come in and he smells that we're cooking in our room. They asked, ‘Hey, is there a party here?’ We say, ‘No, we’re cooking spaghetti. Want some?’ So Joni and Jaco come in. We’re hanging out and Patrick’s playing bass with Jaco. It was a great time.”

Things would turn slightly sour in the US after their 1975 album

Chocolate Kings

, which featured former Acqua Fragile singer and fluent English speaker Bernardo Lanzetti. It featured a sleeve design that didn’t go down too well. “The cover was an American flag with chocolate inside, but the flag wrapper has been thrown away,” Djivas explains. “We really didn’t understand the weight of an Italian band in the US making fun of America.” A focus on foreign territories meant they didn’t put out an Italian version of the record, meaning their profile also slipped back home.

1977’s release

Jet Lag

would prove to be their last sung in English, as Lanzetti departed, and drummer Di Cioccio followed

Phil Collins

route to the lead singer’s mic, and they concentrated on rebuilding their fanbase at home. A pair of records backing Italian folk troubadour Fabrizio De André helped, and they consolidated their position as one of Italy’s best-loved rock acts.

It’s been over a decade since their last album of new compositions, and their task wasn’t helped when guitarist Franco Mussida called it a day in 2015, leaving the rump of Djivas and Di Cioccio in creative charge of the band. But every cloud… “The new guitar player, Marco Sfogli, is from Naples” says Djivas. “Neapolitans have a lot of heart – they’re very emotional people. So he’s a ridiculously good technical player who can do anything, but he also plays great melodies, and we love that.”

They cut off the lights twice because I didn’t pay the bills. Not because I couldn’t, but because I was so focused on the album

While Sfogli is barely half the age of his new bandmates, he’s of a generation who continue to carve out a strong reputation across Europe, helped by a thriving scene back home (covered, we might add, by the Italian equivalent of this magazine,

Prog Italia

). So do Djivas and Di Cioccio hear their influence among the latest crop of Italian bands? “I didn’t listen to anything in the last year,” says Di Cioccio, “and that’s deliberate, because I don’t want to be influenced. Writing songs, arrangements, writing lyrics in Italian, writing in English – it takes focus!”

“I’m the same,” says Djivas. “They cut off the lights in my house twice because I didn’t pay the bills. Not because I couldn’t, but because I was so focused on the album!”

That “no pain, no gain” philosophy has borne fruit, in the shape of an album (albums) that can stand proudly alongside the records with which they made their reputation all those years ago. “For us, the album is a positive journey,” Di Cioccio says. “We start the album with

You’re Not An Island

, and then the last lines are: ‘

I’m feeling like a god!

’”

And who can deny him such feelings? In terms of European prog at least, PFM deserve a bit of deification.

pending_news.title: Blast Worship: Bladda
pending_news.rss_body:
Where they from?

Dallas, Texas. The New York Jets have lost three in a row but the New York Rangers are 3-1, you gotta take what you can get. New York’s goaltender, the legendary Igor Shesterkin, even scored a goal! That surely makes up for the fact that Aaron Glenn has no idea what he’s doing, right? RIGHT?!

Why the hype?

The state of Texas right now is home to a thriving mince/grindcore scene that rivals anywhere else in the world currently, and

Bladda

remain at the heart of the movement. The band churns out a putrid whirlwind of slimy west coast-influenced crusty grindcore that knows when to stop and take a moment to pound you into submission with some seriously tasty OOMPA-OOMPA beats. Combine that with some off-putting samples and a delightfully absurdist name and WA LA, we have a winner.

Latest release?

Heinous Methods of Cranial Disposal

, self-released. This is low IQ-music in the best way possible: just all blasts and then lumbering crust breakdowns, all mixed together in a putrid stew of down-shifted vocals. This is the sort of stuff cavemen would bash each other’s skulls into after killing a whale. Were they alive at the same time? IDK, DOESN’T MATTER!

pending_news.title: Watch Nita Strauss return to the stage as Alice Cooper performs halftime stadium show in Las Vegas
pending_news.rss_body:
Guitarist

Nita Strauss

has returned to the stage with

Alice Cooper

for the first time since leaving his band early this year to go on maternity leave.

Strauss, who gave birth to a son in May, joined Cooper onstage at Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas, Nevada, on Sunday, as the singer provided the halftime entertainment at the NFL game between the Kansas City Chiefs and the Las Vegas Raiders.

Posting on Instagram, Strauss wrote, "Quick trip to Vegas for a super fun (but short) Alice Cooper set at Allegiant Stadium Raiders v Chiefs halftime today! Heartbreaking end to the game, but we had a blast."

Strauss – who is a Los Angeles Rams fan – joined Cooper & Co. as they performed three old-school classics:

No More Mr Nice Guy, I'm Eighteen

and

School's Out

.

Alas, their performance failed to inspire the home team, as the Chiefs narrowly defeated the Raiders 30-27.

Strauss will be returning to Las Vegas in November as Cooper resumes his Welcome To My Nightmare residency with magician Criss Angel.

“Nita opened our 2026 touring season in Las Vegas back in March and is now returning to close out 2026 with us there, and we’re really looking forward to welcoming the Hurricane back onto the stage,” said Cooper last month. “Bringing Nita back after she took a break to start a family is the perfect way to wrap up 2026.”

Cooper also resumes his Alice Attic tour later this month, with

Crossbone Skully

guitarist

Anna Cara

retaining her position as Strauss's temporary replacement. Cooper also begins his

UK book tour

this weekend. Full dates below.

Cooper has also announced that he'll be hosting

pending_news.title: Лидер MEGADETH хочет нырнуть поглубже
pending_news.rss_body:
Во время сессии вопросов и ответов перед выступлением MEGADETH 24 сентября в Grammy Museum в Лос-Анджелесе основатель коллектива Dave Mustaine заявил, что по-прежнему держит слово: 17-й студийный альбом, возглавивший чарты, станет для команды последним. Однако в будущем MEGADETH всё же могут выпустить какой-то дополнительный материал.

Рассуждая о творческом процессе, Mustaine объяснил, что в студию коллектив всегда приходит с готовым планом, но иногда планы меняются.

«Мы всегда приходили в студию с подготовленными песнями. Но если ты автор, ты будешь писать. Ты приходишь в студию записывать альбом, и просто взять и выключить творческий поток не так-то легко, смекаете?

Я не могу сказать, сколько мегабайт риффов остаётся в конце наших песен: мы прослушиваем композицию, и тут рождается новая идея. Я или кто-то из ребят говорим: "Промотай до конца, перемотай в самый конец песни", и мы записываем новую идею туда. Когда весь альбом готов, мы возвращаемся и собираем все эти обрывки.

Так что в какой-то момент мы вернёмся к этой записи, посмотрим на все недописанные песни и выясним, что у нас есть. Может быть, мы даже обнаружим новые песни, оставшиеся после сессий».

Позже Mustaine уточнил: если такой материал и увидит свет, то он будет взят из уже записанных сессий.

«У нас есть фрагменты материала, которые остались в конце нескольких треков на разных альбомах, — рассказал он. — Мы можем вернуться и посмотреть, есть ли там что-нибудь стоящее, потому что, чёрт возьми, если там найдётся, скажем, половина "Holy Wars" и половина "Black Friday", я это выпущу.

Но что касается студийной работы, то моя рука... эта шишка посреди ладони, ей становится всё хуже, и в конце концов это приведёт к тупику. Когда этот день настанет, я пойду на операцию, и либо она поможет, либо нет. А если не поможет — что ж, я прожил чертовски яркую творческую жизнь!»

В августе 2025 года Dave Mustaine объявил, что одноимённый 17-й студийный альбом MEGADETH станет последним. Пластинка, вышедшая в начале 2026 года, дебютировала на первом месте в Billboard 200 в США, а также возглавила чарты ещё в 10 странах мира. Решение уйти на покой он объяснил заболеванием под названием контрактура Дюпюитрена. По данным Mayo Clinic, при нём один или несколько пальцев сгибаются в сторону ладони и не могут полностью разогнуться. Лечение способно облегчить симптомы и замедлить прогрессирование, но излечить контрактуру Дюпюитрена нельзя.

В декабре 2025 года в интервью испанскому каналу MariskalRockTV Mustaine пояснил, что не хочет делать операцию до завершения глобального прощального тура коллектива.

«Я отложу это до тех пор, пока не буду готов рискнуть. Потому что если я попробую сейчас, когда я в форме на 95 процентов, сделаю операцию, и она отбросит меня назад, это будет плохое решение.

А если подождать, пока руки начнут мешать, попробовать, и это не сработает, то тогда я уже объеду все города, со всеми попрощаюсь и не оставлю ничего недосказанным или незавершённым».

В конце 2025 года Mustaine рассказал журналу Kerrang!, что прощальная серия концертов MEGADETH может затянуться надолго.

«Мы всерьёз говорим о гастролях ещё на три-пять лет. А если мы будем ездить так долго, то, чёрт побери, я приближаюсь к дню рождения, о котором даже думать не хочу», — добавил он, имея в виду, что в 2031 году ему исполнится 70 лет.

pending_news.title: DAVID ELLEFSON больше не в DIETH
pending_news.rss_body:
DIETH подписали контракт с Fireflash Records, что открывает новую главу в истории коллектива. Вместе с договором группа представила обновлённый состав: к ней присоединился шведский басист Tobias Cristiansson, известный по работе с GRAVE, NECROPHOBIC и DISMEMBER. Обновлённый коллектив готовится запустить следующий этап своего пути: с новой музыкой, новым видео и вторым студийным альбомом.

Вокалист и гитарист DIETH Guilherme Miranda так прокомментировал сделку с лейблом:

«Это именно тот дом, который нам нужен: здесь разделяют наше видение того, куда можно привести группу. Мы вложили в новую музыку всё сердце и всю душу, и, честно говоря, я просто не могу дождаться того, что мы приготовили. Новый состав, новая музыка, новый альбом — это только начало».

Говоря о приходе Cristiansson'а на смену David Ellefson (экс-MEGADETH), Miranda отметил:

«С огромным удовольствием приветствую в DIETH моего давнего друга Tobias'а. Его послужной список говорит сам за себя, и он идеально вписывается в то, что мы строим. Я безмерно счастлив и горд, что он с нами в этой новой главе».

Первым знакомством с грядущим материалом станет сингл "Pound Of Flesh", один из самых brutal-ных, пожалуй, не подходит; один из самых жестоких на сегодня треков группы, который и откроет новый этап жизни DIETH. Песня выйдет вместе с клипом 16 октября.

Miranda рассказывает:

«"Pound Of Flesh" получилась свирепой, именно такой, какой я и хотел её видеть. И по музыке, и по тексту это одна из моих любимых вещей среди всего, что мы сделали. Я очень взволнован, ведь для DIETH это новая глава. Мне не терпится, чтобы вы услышали и увидели то, над чем мы работали!»

DIETH образовались в 2022 году в польском Гданьске, а в 2023-м выпустили дебютный альбом "To Hell And Back" на Napalm Records. Тем летом коллектив гастролировал по Европе: выступал как хедлайнер на собственных шоу и на фестивалях Graspop Metal Meeting, MotoCultor, Metal On The Hill и Vagos, а также играл на разогреве у TESTAMENT и SEPULTURA.

Североамериканский дебют группа совершила в январе 2024 года, выступив в качестве прямого саппорта METAL ALLEGIANCE в клубе House Of Blues Anaheim в Калифорнии, а в июле того же года отыграла несколько дат в Европе вместе с KK'S PRIEST.

Последний на данный момент сингл DIETH, "Animal Me", вышел в ноябре 2024 года на всех цифровых платформах.

pending_news.title: Новое видео JOHN 5
pending_news.rss_body:
The Phantom, новое видео JOHN 5, доступно для просмотра ниже. Режиссером клипа был Mike Savage партии ударных исполнил Joey Aguirre, а за сведение отвечал Barry Pointer. Этот трек выпущен специально по случаю выпуска новых именных гитар.

Fender Musical Instruments Corporation (FMIC) и Fender Custom Shop (FCS) объявили о выпуске трёх новых сигнатурных Telecaster, посвящённых искусству John 5, не признающему жанровых границ: Fender John 5 Phantom Telecaster, Fender John 5 Ghost Telecaster и Fender Custom Shop John 5 "Phantom" Telecaster. Каждая из гитар передаёт отдельную грань технического мастерства, неповторимого стиля и музыкальной разносторонности John 5'а, делая его фирменное звучание и дизайн доступными большему числу музыкантов в разных ценовых категориях.

«Не знаю, то ли Telecaster выбрала меня, то ли я её, — сказал John 5. — Меня так тянуло к этой форме.

С самого детства Fender был для меня вершиной, лучшим из лучшего, и я мечтал только об одном: чтобы у меня была идеальная гитара и чтобы она радовала и других людей».

Подход John 5 к Telecaster демонстрирует безграничную универсальность инструмента, выводя его культовый дизайн на смелую новую территорию. Он одинаково уверенно чувствует себя и в шреддинге, залитом дисторшном, и в кантри-технике чикен-пикинга, а всей своей карьерой доказывает: для него нет закрытых жанров, стилей и настроений. Преданный поклонник Telecaster с юных лет, он благодаря технически сложной, театральной игре стал одним из самых узнаваемых гитаристов рока.

«John 5 — один из самых самобытных гитаристов современности: он выводит Telecaster за пределы жанров и условностей, и эти три инструмента отражают такую разносторонность, — отметил Джастин Норвелл, директор Fender по гитарным продуктам.

Возвращение Ghost в линейку Fender делает его сигнатурный дизайн доступнее для более широкого круга игроков. Вместе эта коллекция даёт поклонникам любого уровня возможность подключиться к его звуку».

Три сигнатурные модели переводят звук и визуальный стиль John 5 в самостоятельные инструменты, от основной линейки Fender до Fender Custom Shop:

John 5 Phantom Telecaster

Хард-роковая версия классической Telecaster от John 5. Гитара выполнена в притягательном чёрном цвете с головкой грифа в тон. Здесь сочетаются хамбакеры DiMarzio D Activator и тремоло Floyd Rose FRTS2000 Special Series, что даёт мощный выходной сигнал и возможность экстремального изменения высоты тона.

Минималистичная компоновка органов управления, включающая единственную ручку громкости и кнопку килсвитч, оставляет фокус на самой игре, а обтекаемый дизайн выводит Telecaster на смелую новую территорию.

John 5 Ghost Telecaster

Аскетичная Telecaster с высоким выходным сигналом, созданная под фирменное звучание John 5. Ghost продолжает линейку Fender в притягивающем взгляд отделке Arctic White с головкой грифа в тон, хромированной фурнитурой и красными акцентами.

Корпус из ньято придаёт модели особое ощущение в руках, а хамбакеры DiMarzio D Activator выдают мощные, насыщенные гейном тона, которыми знаменит John 5. Упрощённая схема управления с единственной ручкой громкости и килсвитчем сохраняет сосредоточенность дизайна и готовность к сцене.

Fender Custom Shop John 5 "Phantom" Telecaster

Эта модернизированная Telecaster, созданная в Fender Custom Shop, сочетает глянцево-чёрный двухсоставной корпус из отборной ольхи с Ultra Contours и кленовый гриф с профилем Modern "C". Накладка грифа из эбена с плоским ламинированием имеет составной радиус 10"–14" и 22 ладов medium jumbo.

Пара хамбакеров DiMarzio D Activator обеспечивает собранные, мощные тона, а двойной тремоло Floyd Rose Original позволяет экстремально менять высоту звука, сохраняя стабильность строя. Среди дополнительных премиальных деталей: боковые маркеры Luminlay, чёрная фурнитура, запирающиеся колки и сатиновая уретановая отделка грифа.

pending_news.title: David Lee Roth self-diagnoses his own genius on Eat 'Em And Smile
pending_news.rss_body:
Van Halen - Eat 'Em And Smile

(Image credit: Warner Bros)

Yankee Rose

Shyboy

I'm Easy

Ladies' Nite in Buffalo?

Goin' Crazy!

Tobacco Road

Elephant Gun

Big Trouble

Bump And Grind

That's Life

Spontaneous, raw and a bloody good laugh into the bargain, David Lee Roth's

Eat ’Em & Smile

was a massive ‘fuck you’ to those who viewed Diamond Dave's exit from

Van Halen

as a rock’n’roll suicide by any other name.

The album teamed the Sunset Strip’s biggest ego with the best rock musicians on the planet: guitarist

Steve Vai

, bassist Billy Sheehan, and drummer Gregg Bissonette, who unleashed a brash, loud and colourful collection of Halen-esque party-influenced hard rock.

It holds its own against any Van Halen record –

Yankee Rose

features a jaw-dropping ‘talking guitar’ intro from Vai – and a charisma-bomb performance from Roth, while

Shyboy

(a cover of a song by Sheehan's previous band, Talas) and

Goin’ Crazy

aren’t far behind, but the ever-unpredictable singer wasn't entirely happy.

"It ran into the dead end that is rock-fusion jazz-blues something or other, aka ‘widdley widdley’," Roth told

Classic Rock

. "When the guitarist starts going ‘widdley widdley’ it’s a symptom. When I made those records with Steve it was an effort to get him to go under the bar; consolidate; give your guitar solo a beginning, middle and end.

"What is the development of the character here? Is this guitar solo the same guy we met in the last three songs? Perhaps one is never so much oneself as when wearing the mask. And Steve’s mask is that there is something greater than writing songs and simple emotional content."

Stream on Spotify

Stream on Apple Music

Every week, Album of the Week Club listens to and discusses the album in question, votes on how good it is, and publishes our findings, with the aim of giving people reliable reviews and the wider rock community the chance to contribute.

Join the group now

.

Other albums released in July 1986

Knocked Out Loaded - Bob Dylan

Orgasmatron - Motörhead

Landing On Water - Neil Young

The Bridge - Billy Joel

Lightning Strikes - Loudness

Life's Rich Pageant - R.E.M.

QR III - Quiet Riot

East of Midnight - Gordon Lightfoot

No Guru, No Method, No Teacher - Van Morrison

Should The World Fail To Fall Apart - Peter Murphy

Sound Of Confusion - Spacemen 3

What they said...

"In the strictest metal tradition, many tracks are just frenzied riffs with Roth rapping on top. And surprisingly enough, there's nothing here as slick as the two singles on Van Halen's post-Roth LP. Luckily, Vai's guitar work provides a rough enough roller-coaster ride to counter the lack of more melodic hooks." (

Rolling Stone

)

"With everybody from Patti to Belinda to Peter to Eldra kissing pop's ass, Roth gives it a pinch and keeps on trucking. Maybe because he lived out his wimpier fantasies on last year's EP, here he's free to mastermind his own piece of multiplatinum potential. Sure he covers

That's Life

, but he also assembles a metal band that'll cut old buddies: Maynard Ferguson drummer, cult heaven bassist, and on guitar former Zappa and Lydon sideman Steve Vai, who splits the difference between parody and virtuosity." (

Robert Christgau

)

"The "diamond" one set out to out-Van Halen Van Halen with his band's first effort,

Eat 'Em and Smile

, a more than adequate substitute for the overtly commercial tendencies of the "new and improved" original. Why mess with a winning recipe, indeed. Guitarist Steve Vai, bassist Billy Sheehan, and drummer Gregg Bissonette sound perfectly at home aping their boss's old cronies on such sizzling party anthems as

Shyboy

and

Elephant Gun.

" (

AllMusic

)

What you said...

Nick Tedds:

I remember thinking at the time of release that

Eat ‘Em And Smile

was an excellent album in parts. Lead single

Yankee Rose

is innovative/gimmicky enough to stand out from the crowd,

Shyboy

an opportunity for the Vai/Sheehan combo to showcase their twiddly histrionics, and

Ladies Nite in Buffalo

has a huge funky groove that is different but works well alongside the aforementioned opening tracks.

Goin’ Crazy

is also catchy enough.

After that though... I’m not a fan of the lounge-swing approach of

I’m Easy,

and

That’s Life

. The cover of

Tobacco Road

is fairly pointless, and

Bump And Grind

offers nothing new at all. It’s not often that I think an album of just over half an hour in length may have been better if it had been trimmed a little! But then again, that’s exactly what I thought about Roth’s last effort with Van Halen,

1984,

although, as with that album, the musicianship is undeniably of the highest quality and Ted Templeman’s production is top-notch.

Adam Ranger

: Controversial opinion: Diamond Dave is not as good as he thinks he is. The first three Van Halen albums were great, a sum of their parts rather than just one individual.

But I find this a bit one-dimensional and uninspiring. Great musicians on it, no question. But Dave having "fun" does not mean a good record. No song on this album stands out, and I would be quite happy not to hear it again.

Mark Herrington

: Mixed feelings about this one. There are some good tracks and great guitar pyrotechnics throughout. However, the sheer amount of covers at the expense of original material, and the weaker second half, drains some of that initial enthusiasm.

I love the punchy party rock on

Yankee Rose

, a great track and a great start, the standout track by miles here.

Shyboy

is a good display of guitar pyrotechnics, although not as catchy as

Yankee Rose.

The bluesy cover

I’m Easy

is a bit Dad Rock, but the guitar is great.

Ladies Night

lacks oomph, with good guitar.

Goin' Crazy

is a return to energetic party rock, with a weakish chorus rescued by great guitar.

Tobacco Road

– another cover – ushers in the weaker second half, and it's better than anything that follows. The tracks are just average from here, and finish with another cover in

That's Life

.

Some good stuff, some great guitar, but the album is short on ideas and consistency. If anything, it just gets me reaching for my copy of

Van Halen I

, to hear it done properly.

Chris Elliott

: In simple terms, it sounds like Van Halen. So that pretty much tells you if you'll like it. It's harmless FM rock that passes by without annoying or engaging. At my age, I don't think I'm about to be converted

Chris Downie

: Given the endlessly-publicised fallout over the split in the Van Halen camp in 1985, it was inevitable that both David Lee Roth's full-length debut and the first 'Van Hagar' effort

5150

would be intertwined with one another, far too often compared directly, as opposed to being viewed as distinct entities in their own right and enjoyed (or otherwise) on their own merits.

While the revamped Van Halen decided, at first, to continue the musical path taken on the mega-selling

1984

album (before paring back the keyboards on the provocatively titled follow-up

OU812

a few years later, and even more so on the heavier remaining 'Van Hagar' outings), Roth decided to go all-in with his cabaret clown show, albeit to mildly entertaining effect.

Where his solo career fell short, however, was in his failure to evolve beyond his first three solo efforts, culminating in the impressive

A Little Ain't Enough,

which was underpinned by the incredible talent of the young Jason Becker.

While the debut EP, replete with Beach Boys tribute, gave hints of what was to come, this full-length hits the spot when on point (

Yankee Rose

needs no introduction, but

Shyboy

is also impressive) but tails off in the second half. Moreover, its sparse running time of 31 minutes – two tracks of which are cover versions – treads the same path that held back the otherwise brilliant innovation of early Van Halen. Love it or hate it, the Van Hagar lineup evolved impressively and remained on top, while Roth's career stagnated and ultimately faded into a novelty act by the mid-90s.

Decades further down the line and taking a fresh perspective, if

Eat 'Em And Smile

does one thing in 2026, it tells us the original Van Halen line up were a product of their time, an exciting breath of fresh air that ushered in the American 80's metal scene two years before that decade even began, but which also burned out just as the second wave they heavily influenced, such as Dokken, Ratt, Twisted Sister et al, were hitting their peak. Despite their individual brilliance, they were somehow greater than the sum of their parts, but when divided, it was Roth who ultimately fell by the wayside, into self-parody. 7/10.

Gary Claydon

: Flawed but fun offering from the King of good-time metal. Neverthess,

Eat 'Em and Smile

is more hit than miss, thanks in large part to a genuinely killer band (ably aided and abetted by Ted Templeman's spot-on production), with Vai's guitar the real star of the show.

Raucous album opener, the classic

Yankee Rose

is a perfect illustration of Diamond Dave's technicolour, larger-than-life approach to rock'n'roll and the obvious stand-out track. The easy strut and groove of

Ladies' Night In Buffalo

runs it close, while

Big Trouble

has a lesser-spotted semi-serious DLR lyric. Elsewhere, there is plenty of energy, but a heavy whiff of filler lingers, and the covers are a waste of the talent on show.

Brian Carr:

A lot of memories for me on this one. I saw some great shows in my first three years of concert-going, and DLR on this tour was one of my favourites - his band were white hot! Steve Vai is in my top ten favourite guitar players; Billy Sheehan is almost certainly in my top five favourite bass players. The videos were loads of fun.

Ladies Night In Buffalo

was the second or third song I learned on bass. And, of course, I absolutely loved the

Eat 'Em And Smile

record.

Times and musical tastes change over the decades, though. I found and bought a used vinyl copy in recent years, but haven’t listened to it often. The album is still fun, and the performances are still electric. I still love Vai and Sheehan, and Bissonette is a fantastic drummer and perfect fit for the band. But listening 40 years later(!!!), it’s really hard to forget how poorly Dave’s schtick aged.

I’m Easy

and

That’s Life

may be fun, but on a record barely longer than 30 minutes, it screams padding and shows that Dave’s idea of entertainment is simultaneously inside

and

outside the norm. It’s also hard to ignore that

Eat ‘Em And Smile

was, in my opinion, the apex - it all went downhill from here. Five years later, I saw Roth again in what I will always remember as one of the worst concerts I’ve ever seen.

All of that said, it’s still great to hear Roth in his ADHD prime, together with one of the greatest rock lineups.

Philip Qvist

: It is a fun album, with great guitar pyrotechnics from Steve Vai backed by a solid rhythm section of Billy Sheehan and Gregg Bissonette, while Diamond Dave does what he does best, i.e. being Diamond Dave. None of the songs should be taken seriously, which was probably the real purpose of

Eat 'Em And Smile

, hence the cover versions.

There is nothing here that surprises me, and the songs are exactly what you expect from David Lee Roth, with song titles such as

Bump And Grind, Elephant Gun

and Ladies

Night in Buffalo

, with lyrics to match. The standout track is the opener,

Yankee Rose

(which I believe is a tribute to the Statue of Liberty).

So this is a fun and enjoyable album, but it's also a disposable one. The fact is that David Lee Roth needed Van Halen as much as Van Halen needed him (and this is not a slight against Sammy Hagar). No more than a 7 from me this week, but at least this album title inspired "Van Hagar" to name their next album

OU812

.

Mike Canoe

: I love it, I love it, and no one can change my mind.

Eat ‘Em And Smile

finds David Lee Roth trying to out Van Halen Van Halen by building his own perfect beast and I, for one, think, on this one album, that he succeeded, especially compared to the recently released

5150

and its emphasis on ballads and,

gasp

, pop songcraft.

Steve Vai made the lead guitar ridiculously

Hot For Teacher

fun again on songs like the giddy opener

Yankee Rose

and sex positive

Bump And Grind

. Fellow recruit Billy Sheehan was referred to in the music press at the time as the "Eddie Van Halen of bass." And while drummer Gregg Bissonette didn't have the name recognition of the rest of the band, he certainly knew what he was doing, whether on ravers like

Shyboy

or

Elephant Gun

or lounge lizards like

I'm Easy

or

That's Life

.

The band brings out the best in Roth. Roth was Van Halen's hype man (and he knew it), and he brings that same manic energy and showmanship here while still showing a (relative) maturity on

Ladies' Nite in Buffalo?

and

Big Trouble

. Interestingly, I used to hate

Goin' Crazy

because of those %$#@ing keyboards, but now it's one of my favourites.

Roth knew from the success of

Diver Down

that the majority of fans don't care if a song's a cover if it's "Van Halen'd" enough, and that's what he and his new band do with

Tobacco Road

. I don't think Roth ever got enough credit for his sense of humour or eclectic taste in cover choices. It's not like a hard rock band covering Frank Sinatra was a shoo-in for commercial success until Roth already proved it could be done with

Ain't Got Nobody/Just a Gigolo

.

Roth has been slagged since Van Halen's inception as a terrible singer, and I absolutely do not give a shit. He made rock'n'roll more fun than just about anybody before or since.

His prevailing fatal flaw has always been that he thinks he is the sole genius in the room instead of a vital part of a team. The ridiculously steep decline of his solo career indicates his need for talented collaborators. Roth had the ability to make already good things great. He thought he was coffee, but he was just the cream. (No,

you're

making it gross.)

Still, I would argue that

Eat 'Em and Smile

was the last great Van Halen album until 2012's

A Different Kind of Truth

. Roth, like the rest of Van Halen, was closely identified with the big, bright 1980s. It’s unlikely that a mid-’90s VH album with Roth would have fared much better than

Balance

or

VHIII

. Still, Roth may have been the fourth most musically talented member of any Van Halen lineup he was in, but he was always the most fun.

Marco Edwards:

Great album.

John Davidson

: We all loved Van Halen, but they never really topped their explosive debut, and while

1984

was a chart-bothering return to form, the writing was on the wall that DLR and the Van Halens were on different trajectories. Dave wanted pop hits, and with a couple of hit solo singles under his belt, he left the band to set out on his own.

It's ironic then that

Eat 'Em And Smile

sounds like a more natural follow-up to

1984

than

5150

. Though

5150

scuppered any hope EVH had of avoiding the charts with its AOR sound and the solid punch of Sammy Hagar.

It's not as if DLR had to downgrade the musicianship on his solo run either, though. Steve Vai brings the guitar chops that are every bit as good as Eddie's, Sheehan is arguably a better bassist than Michael Anthony, and Gregg Bissonette is no slouch on the drums either.

The two standouts are

Yankee Rose

and

Tobacco Road

, but songs like

Elephant Gun

rip along like the best early Van Halen, mixing guitar wig-outs and bass runs with the staccato drumming of

Hot For Teacher

.

I didn't pay this much heed at the time, but it brought a smile today, and at just over 30 minutes long, it doesn't hang around long enough to get tiresome. 8/10.

Mark Veitch

: I loved this album when I was in my teens, but then I also loved Skittles back then too! For such a great band, disappointing they could only come up with six new songs and padded out the album with covers.

Yankee Rose

and

Ladies Night In Buffalo

are the stand-out tracks, and live they were a top band, but this album doesn’t get many spins these days, and Dave's career quickly tailed off in line with his hairline and the 80s.

Adam Halpin

: Great music and awful lyrics.

David R. Howard

: This is a great record. I still listen to it.

Nigel Mawdsley

: I do like, and indeed own, some of Dave Lee Roth's solo albums but find

Eat 'Em And Smile

a little one-dimensional. There's no denying the superb musicianship and production, but I found the original songs very 'samey' and merging into one.

The cover of

Tobacco Road

seems to get stuck in a similar groove to the rest of the album; it's a great song, but I always feel there's something lacking when I play it.

Generally the album's okay, but Diamond Dave, as a solo artist, went on to produce better material. 6 out of 10.

Erik Schiavo

: This Buffoon's last shining moment. This tour was great.

Greg Schwepe

: So, still trying to figure this out.

Huge

Van Halen fan (of both eras) since day one. Love DLR and his sense of humor, swagger, attitude, and the overall concept of “Dave Being Dave.” But I did not rush out and buy this (or any other DLR solo albums) at the time it was released. It wasn’t until I had access to his entire catalogue via the streaming platforms that I actually listened to

Eat 'Em And Smile

in its entirety. But, at the time I liked everything I heard on the radio or saw on MTV. Probably more MTV.

Maybe I wasn’t too excited about him being backed by another group of musicians besides Eddie, Alex, and Mike? Which is silly, because, wow, did he enlist some musician firepower on this album or what? Or maybe I was staying loyal to Brand Van Halen even though one of the main ingredients had been swapped out and the recipe had changed. Or was it just that in some cases I have little interest in a solo album from someone even though they were a member of one of my favourite bands?

The first thing I noticed when listening again was the brevity of the album at 30 minutes. Get in, state your musical case, then get out.

This album runs the gamut from full-on, hard-rocking, guitar-fueled songs (

Yankee Rose, Goin’ Crazy, Elephant Gun

), a little jump blues (

I’m Easy

), and the show tune vibe of album closer

That’s Life

complete with strings and horns. All done DLR style. I tend to think Dave adheres to my own personal motto: “anything worth doing is worth overdoing.” So he’s all over the board here in those 30 minutes, but it’s all just enough and not too much. I must have listened to this 2-3 times today and have come to appreciate it more. Nothing “dark” here, just Dave bringing the

fun

.

And since this was released about four months after

5150

, you’re going to get the inevitable “well, which one was better?” discussions. And I say they’re too hard to compare, as the difference between them was way too far apart.

8 out of 10 on this one for me. “Dave Being Dave” is a good way to spend a half hour.

Mike Sargent:

The only DLR solo album that is worth a spin.

Final score: 7.56 (103 votes cast, total score 779)

pending_news.title: How Deep Purple, Black Sabbath and the California Jam banished Altamont's demons
pending_news.rss_body:
California had been truly rocked – and not in a good way – by the tragic events that occurred at the

Altamont Free Concert in 1969

. Five years later, the rock world was ready to try again with a brand new festival of high-voltage music. Over 250,000 people descended upon the Ontario Motor Speedway in Ontario, California on April 6, 1974 to attend what had been billed simply as the California Jam.

Boasting an eight-band line-up –

Rare Earth

, Earth, Wind & Fire, Eagles, Seals & Crofts, Black Oak Arkansas,

Black Sabbath

,

Deep Purple

Mk III and headliners

Emerson, Lake & Palmer

– the first of the two California Jams would prove to be a mammoth affair.

The genesis of the festival was an unusual one. The giant American TV network ABC had a long-running show called

In Concert

, a programme which captured bands of the day live on stage. It was a groundbreaking idea, since the show was simultaneously broadcast live on FM radio.

One thing led to another, and the executives at ABC turned to

In Concert

producer Don E Branker and suggested that they would like to host a rock’n’roll festival in California and broadcast it. Branker had had experience in promoting rock shows (primarily on the East coast of the US), and he thought that the Ontario Speedway, located about 50 miles outside of Los Angeles, might prove the perfect location to resurrect the Californian rock festival.

Along with his fellow co-producers Lenny Stogel (who died in an aeroplane accident in 1979) and Sandy Feldman, Branker started to investigate the feasibility of a festival at the speedway.

“We went out to Ontario,” Branker told DJ Mike Stark earlier this year. “And we told them that we wanted to put on a music show. The truth of the matter is that we didn’t say the word ‘festival’, since that was a dirty word after Altamont and Woodstock. And we told them that we wanted to put on acts like the Jackson 5 and the Osmonds, and that it would only be that kinda show.”

The subterfuge worked, and ABC and the producers were granted the requisite permits to arrange the “music show”.

“We then went back three weeks later and told them, ‘Well, we couldn’t get those acts, but we have got Deep Purple, Black Sabbath and Emerson Lake & Palmer,” laughed Branker. “Luckily the police chief out there had never heard of them and he said ‘OK, that sounds fine.’ Later on, he learned that Deep Purple and Black Sabbath were blacklisted, that they were kinda rebellious.”

The crowd at the first California Jam, 1974

(Image credit: ABC Photo Archives/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

It was too late though, the permits were issued and the show went ahead as planned. Thankfully, the police chief’s fears were unwarranted and the day passed peacefully. Crowd control was something that was foremost in the promoter’s mind, as Lenny Stogel recalled shortly before his death. “When I knew I was putting on a show for 200,000 young people, I didn’t want anything popping off unexpected. I wanted to be in total control and know exactly what was happening that moment and what would be happening in the next few hours. Two hundred thousand kids was a big responsibility. I used to get a funny feeling in my stomach whenever I thought about it. I had to be in control – for the preservation of my sanity.”

But that didn’t mean that the first Jam was uneventful. And despite Stogel wanting to be in control, that didn’t mean there weren’t gatecrashers.

The first notable happening – for a rock show at least – was that opening act

Rare Earth

actually took to the stage 15 minutes ahead of schedule at 9.45am.

Emerson Lake & Palmer may have been the headline band, but it was a newly invigorated Deep Purple who were the scene stealers of the day. The official attendance figure of California Jam was 250,000 but “there were maybe 350,000 or 400,000 people there altogether. The fences came down and they all rushed in,” recalls

Glenn Hughes

, who joined Purple as bassist/vocalist in 1973. “The California Jam was really, really huge. It was a great moment for us.”

As it was their brainchild, major portions of the California Jam were broadcast live on America’s ABC TV channel. The network took a gamble on rock and managed to get four special programmes out of it. Purple’s performance was truly sensational, and clearly won ABC ratings points.

Fuelled by backstage aggravation, their set climaxed in an orgy of destruction by guitarist

Ritchie Blackmore

. As the epic

Space Truckin’

came to a close, he

smashed his Fender Stratocaster repeatedly into a camera operator’s lens

. He then went on to destroy several more guitars before a huge explosion in his Marshall stacks set his hair on fire.

“It went a bit too far,” remembers

David Coverdale

, who was plucked from obscurity to become Purple’s vocalist for the

Burn

album.

“There was too much explosive. It looks great, I agree, but Ritchie got burned. Thankfully it was nothing too serious.”

It did look impressive though, and unequivocally made them band of the day. Footage from Purple’s performance has subsequently been released on DVD. “I love playing in front of a lot of people,” says Hughes. “You can see that from the DVD footage. I was ready for that. I was born to play the California Jam.”

“When I saw the DVD I realised I learned shitloads from that performance,” added Coverdale. “It helped set me on my way with Whitesnake.”

There was also something very unusual about Coverdale’s performance that day. Not in terms of his singing, but rather what he had in his pocket.

“I remember having a million-dollar cheque in the arse pocket of my jeans when we headlined the California Jam. Because I was on camera the whole time I thought that was the safest place to keep it. It was a lot of money in those days.”

Bernie Leadon (left) and Don Felder onstage with Eagles

(Image credit: ABC Photo Archives/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

The day was split very deliberately into two halves; the first four bands on the bill were mellower, almost pop-based groups. And as the day progressed, the heavier and louder the music got.

In the first batch of four, you may have noticed that there was a small band that went by the name of

Eagles

. In 1974, they were little more than a fledgling group, and the California Jam would be one of the very few performances when the soft rock band would play with Jackson Browne on keyboards.

It took the organisers three weeks of preparation for California Jam – the Ontario Speedway was a virtually empty swathe of land. Everything had to be brought in especially for the event. Power, water, staging, the whole lot. Given the hi-tech nature of the show – and the fact that it was being done especially for broadcast, many considerations were made that have since become the template for large festival dates.

Realising that an idle crowd is a potentially dangerous crowd, the organisers needed a method by which the transition between bands on stage was as quick and seamless as possible. As part of a ground-breaking idea, sections of the stage were mounted on railway tracks, enabling portions of it to be moved into position with ease (and in super quick time). In fact, turnaround time between bands throughout the day had been kept to about ten minutes. All was going swimmingly until Sabbath came off the stage after their amazing performance.

“English acts are very competitive,” explained Don Branker. “It goes back to the days when they used to play the same clubs, and Sabbath and Purple always had a rivalry because they were both at the beginning of heavy metal.”

Deep Purple had decided that they didn’t want to go on stage until after darkness had fallen, as they had a few surprises for the promoter. Namely, they had pyrotechnics ready to go. And they couldn’t stick the idea of being upstaged by

Ozzy Osbourne

and his band of doom merchants.

Ozzy Osbourne salutes the crowd at the 1974 California Jam

(Image credit: ABC Photo Archives/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

With California Jam being a success – it was the largest-grossing concert to date – the most natural idea was to organise a follow-up. And on March 18, 1978, the largest sound system that had ever been built for a festival was cranked up and ready to go.

Using a similar formula to its predecessor, California Jam II revolved around a nine-band bill. This time around it was the turn of Ted Nugent,

Aerosmith

,

Heart

,

Foreigner

, Dave Mason, Bob Welch – with special guests Stevie Nicks and Mick Fleetwood, Frank Marino & Mahogany Rush and Rubicon.

It looked great on paper, but there was one thing beyond the promoters’ control that threatened to mar the second Cali Jam – an uncustomary glitch in the glorious California sunshine. For three consecutive weekends prior to the Jam, Southern California had been struck with rain. Lots and lots of rain. And as any veteran of British festivals will confirm, rain can have a nasty habit of spoiling even the greatest of events. However, once again the gods were on the side of rock’n’roll, and for that single Saturday in a rainy year, the clouds kept their peace.

The staging was configured so that while one band was playing, another could be prepared to minimise the time between band switchovers. Once again, the organisers reckoned on about a quarter of a million people in attendance at the gig. Officially at least. The bands, however, thought otherwise.

“It was just huge,” Heart’s Ann Wilson recalled in 1989. “There must have been about 350,000 people there. It was like standing in the middle of a small city. I’d never seen anything like it.”

In terms of catching the public’s imagination, the bill for California Jam II was perfect, as Branker told Stark. “We were real lucky,” he explained. “The top four acts on that show were Aerosmith, Ted Nugent, Foreigner and Heart. We booked the show in December and by the time the show came round, four of the top five albums in the nation were Foreigner’s first album, Heart’s first album, Nugent’s

Cat Scratch Fever

album and

Draw The Line

from Aerosmith, so we really lucked into that being so hot at the time.”

Luck may have had something to do with it, but there can be no denying that both California Jams were examples of how a huge outdoor rock festival could (and should) be run. And the artists agreed.

“I’m lost for words. The kids blow my mind. It was like an ocean of people out there,” Ozzy told a radio interviewer after Sabbath came off stage at the first Jam. “When people’s arms went up in the air… I’m just knocked out by it all. If only every open-air rock show could go half as good as this. This is where it’s at, y’know…”

pending_news.title: Lamb Of God's Randy Blythe on doing what he does best
pending_news.rss_body:
Lamb Of God

frontman Randy Blythe admits he wouldn't describe himself as a "really good musician" – but he knows he's "really good at being in Lamb Of God."

The vocalist believes that never thinking of himself as the best at anything helps him to continue on a path of continual improvement, insisting that the moment you think of yourself as the best, "then you're shit."

Blythe tells Metal On Top: "I'm only good at one or two things, so I might as well just do what I'm good at.

I'm a pretty good writer and I'm a pretty good photographer. Not the best in the world. But I'm pretty good at being in Lamb of God.

"I'm not gonna say I'm a really good musician, but I'm really good at being in Lamb Of God."

He adds that when you think you are perfect, you lose the drive required to truly deliver.

"That's when your talent abandons you," he says. "When you become convinced of your own genius or whatever and that you can do no wrong, then you're not striving anymore.

"As an artist, whatever medium you're working in, in the moment of creation, you're struggling with yourself. You're trying to understand yourself and your place within the world. And in that moment, you're also trying to move beyond your own talent level.

"So, every time we make a record, I'm trying to do something I didn't think I could do before, not reinventing the wheel. And every time I write, I'm trying to write above my talent level, rather than just sitting in a sort of medium, because that's when you get lazy."

In the wide-ranging interview, Blythe also discusses his sparing use of clean vocals and how he avoids being affected by online negativity. View video of the full interview below.

Lamb Of God released their latest album

Into Oblivion

earlier this year.

pending_news.title: The wild 1970s glam rock classic inspired by The Beatles, Wagner… and Humphrey Bogart
pending_news.rss_body:
It took weeks to record, with an odd choice of producer and no record label involved. But it kick-started an iconic career. The album was 1972’s self-titled debut by

Roxy Music

, and it contained all the elements that would make them legendary. And for guitarist

Phil Manzanera

it was a hectic time. “I was only officially confirmed in the band on February 14, 1972, and a month later we were in the studio.”

Manzanera had auditioned the previous October, but lost out to former Nice man David O’List. But when the band played in front of EG Management in early February ’72, there was a fight between O’List and drummer Paul Thompson. As a result, EG took on the band but insisted on O’List going.

So in came Manzanera, joining Thompson, frontman Bryan Ferry, bassist Graham Simpson, synth player Brian Eno and saxophonist Andy Mackay. And, funded by EG, Roxy went to Command Studios in central London on March 14, working with producer Pete Sinfield, best known as the lyricist for

King Crimson

. “EG managed him, so they kept it in the family. I don’t why he was chosen, but the good thing is that Pete let us get on with it.”

Roxy recorded live in the studio, with few overdubs. But the band had rehearsed so much that they were ready to do it this way. “We were a band of inspired amateurs back then, who worked very hard and had lots of enthusiasm. And the album has a charm all of its own as a result.”

Roxy Music in 1972: (from left) Paul Thompson, Brian Ferry, Andy Mackay, Phil Manzanera, Brian Eno

(Image credit: Gijsbert Hanekroot/Redferns)

The songs were written by Ferry, bearing a number of cinematic references, something that delighted Manzanera. “That’s one of the things the two of us bonded over – we loved films. And to hear something like

2HB

, with its tribute to Humphrey Bogart, or

Chance Meeting

[inspired by the classic movie

Brief Encounter

] was just incredible. Bryan had so many ideas, and I always thought the rest of us provided the music for his words.”

The opening song,

Re-Make/Re-Model

, actually sums up the band’s eclecticism, with nods to

The Beatles

, Duane Eddy and… Wagner. “We all got the chance at the end to do our own thing. It’s a mad journey with lots of energy and it’s so exciting. It immediately says who we were – a band who would try anything."

While Roxy had a big hit with

Virginia Plain

later in 1972, reaching No.4 in the chart, this was recorded four months after the album and not included in the track listing. “In those days, we liked to keep singles separate and not feature them on albums.”

Apart from the music, what immediately stands out is the cover, featuring model Kari-Ann Muller. It set Roxy apart from almost everyone. “This cover was so striking that we’re going to be using it to promote our January UK tour – it still looks so good even now.”

The album was eventually released through Island, thanks to a licensing deal done by EG. “We got £5,000 from the label for a five-year lease. In those days, that was very innovative. I know EG had to fight to persuade some people at Island to put this out. But it did well for them.”

Roxy Music

reached No.10 in the UK charts, selling over 100,000 copies. As Manzanera concludes: “This was just the beginning. The rest is history.”

Originally published in Classic Rock issue 150 (March 2010)

pending_news.title: Rick Wakeman is exploring Mars and playing a concert for bears in Vietnam. What on earth?
pending_news.rss_body:
Rick Wakeman

has been to Mars. Well, kinda. The veteran keyboard player recently visited the Airbus Space Facility in Stevenage to film promo videos for his latest album,

Return To The Red Planet

, a sequel to 2020’s critically praised

The Red Planet

.

“Airbus has its own [recreation of] Mars; it’s where all of the craft that go into space are tested out,” Wakeman tells

Classic Rock

. “I did check my British Airways air miles and there were not enough for a trip to Mars, so they kindly allowed us to go in and do some filming. I do have a very genuine interest in the subject, so it was great to spend time talking to all of the technicians and scientists there.”

He continues: “Ever since [Russian cosmonaut] Yuri Gagarin went up and back [in 1961] I’ve been fascinated with space, and I’ve got some good friends at NASA. Photographs of the Russians’ first mission were grainy, understandably, but since then technology has improved things phenomenally. And with so much new information I thought: ‘Crikey, there’s another album here’. For instance, Mars almost certainly used to be a blue planet like Earth, and where there’s water it’s pretty certain there will also be life. My pal David [Bowie] was right.”

Speaking of the Bowie, Wakeman’s nine-track

Return To The Red Planet

features a rather wonderful selection titled Bowie’s

Vision

. With its false ending and uplifting choral climax, it’s a lovely tribute to Wakeman’s old friend, some of whose albums he played on and whose 1971 hit single

Life On Mars?

was enhanced by a distinctive piano solo from Wakeman.

“I’m glad you like that one,” he says of Bowie’s

Vision

, smiling. “It’s a tongue-in-cheek story of what David did, and I love the [choral] part at the end.”

(Image credit: Michael Inns)

Described as a “progressive work that fuses science, imagination and musical virtuosity”,

Return To The Red Planet

is released on October 16 via Madfish. It was created along with Wakeman’s regular backing collective The English Rock Ensemble, featuring Mollie Marriott (daughter of late Small Faces and

Humble Pie

frontman Steve) on lead vocals, plus bassist Lee Pomeroy, guitarist Dave Colquhoun and drummer Adam Falkner.

Should the opportunity arise in the future, Wakeman hopes to perform both of his Mars-themed albums together in a single show, although, as he points out, it depends very much on the reaction of the public to the new record. “If it’s only bought by eight people and a dog, that won’t be anywhere enough to sell tickets for a concert,” he notes.

Wakeman has repeatedly spoken of working towards retirement, but his calendar seems to contradict that. In December he and son Oliver undertake A Hint Of Christmas, six festive dates around Britain, followed by 18 UK shows billed as Wizard Of Prog in February and March 2027.

“In October I’m doing STARMUS VIII – The Search For Truth, a big piece for piano and chamber orchestra that’s based on the lectures of [late astrophysicist and cosmologist] Stephen Hawking, which I’m really looking forward to, and also next year I’m headed off to South America,” he explains. “But I am slowing down.”

It’s all set to come to a head on Wakeman’s birthday, May 18, in 2029. “That’s when I turn… oh Crikey,” he calculates theatrically. “Is it eighty-nine? Ninety? A hundred? I dunno. No, it’ll be my ninetieth birthday. That will be the last big bang for me. I hope to go out in style at somewhere like the Royal Albert Hall with lots and lots of friends and special guests on stage. I will keep on making music, there’s still tonnes of stuff left to do, but in terms of touring that will be it. I may still do the occasional concert here and there, but I have to be sensible.”

Before he heads off to rehearse for STARMUS VIII, we have a rumour to run past him: that in September he goes to Vietnam to play piano in an open-air concert for an audience of… bears.

“It’s true,” he affirms. “I’m an ambassador for Animals Asia, which saves moon bears from the dreadful bear bile trade. They go into sanctuaries and get their lives back. The Vietnamese have now banned bear bile farming, but as part of that deal we must look after them. I came up with this silly idea to raise awareness: why don’t I go there and do a concert for the bears? Not for people, but for the actual bears. Obviously I can’t go into the cages,” he says, grinning, “but they’re building a stage and we bring along a grand piano.

“The funny thing is, for the last few months they’ve been playing them some of my piano albums, so that the bears have an idea of what to expect. When I get there they’ll probably turn around and say: ‘Oh shit, it’s him again.’”

Return To The Red Planet is released via Madfish on October 16.

pending_news.title: How Ozzy opened No Rest For The Wicked with an almighty diss track against a disgraced preacher
pending_news.rss_body:
In 1986, televangelist Jimmy Swaggart was on his own personal crusade. He described rock bands and rock magazines as “pornography and degenerative filth which denigrates all the values we hold sacred and is destructive to youth.”

According to a Los Angeles Times news story published that summer, his words and reputation held such weight during the height of the Satanic Panic, that 800 Walmart stores across North America stopped stocking rock and teen magazines. Albums by

Ozzy Osbourne

,

Black Sabbath

,

Mötley Crüe

, and

Judas Priest

were also pulled from the shelves.

“Let’s just say there are scores of magazines like

Hit Parader

, which are sold to teens, that are full of four-letter words and graphic descriptions and language which gives teens the impression that premarital sex and perversion are just fine,” said Swaggart. “I bought a whole stack of magazines last week and they contain lurid pornographic detail about these groups. The whole rock scene – the records, the magazines and the concerts – couldn’t get any worse. They’re taking a deadly toll.”

Ozzy Osbourne holding a cup of tea in the garden of his home in May 1988

(Image credit: Mirrorpix/Getty Images)

When Ozzy Osbourne and his band were working on the follow-up to

The Ultimate Sin

in early 1988, news broke that Swaggart, a first cousin of the problematic rock 'n' roller

Jerry Lee Lewis

, had visited a sex worker in a New Orleans motel. The sound of Ozzy's unmistakable cackle must have been heard across the whole of Los Angeles.

Swaggart made a tearful, televised apology from the Family Worship Center, in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, that February and, in turn, inspired the opening song on

No Rest for The Wicked.

Ozzy's fifth studio album marked the studio debut of his new protégé Jeffrey Phillip Wielandt, a 21-year-old with a mane of blond hair and skills reminiscent of the late

Randy Rhoads

.

Renamed by Ozzy's wife and manager Sharon as

Zakk Wylde

, his recruitment brought a dazzling flair and much-needed crunch to the new material following the dismissal of Jake E. Lee.

“You know, I have a knack for finding great guitarists,” Ozzy told

Guitar World

. “Jake E. Lee, was, and still is a great guitar player. But it was just one of those things that happened. And Zakk would ask me questions about the previous guys, about Randy, about Jake, about Tony [

Iommi

]. He wanted to learn. And he only got better.

“People used to say to me, ‘Why don’t you go for the best soccer player?’ And I’d say, ‘No. I have more fun watching a guy who wants to be the best soccer player develop into him.’ Zakk was that guy.”

The artwork for Ozzy Osbourne's 1988 single, Miracle Man

(Image credit: Epic/CBS)

Zakk's guitar parts on

Miracle Man

were inspired by The

Jimi Hendrix

Experience's 1967 single

Foxy Lady

(or

Foxey Lady

).

"That's why I always tell kids, it's just like cooking," Zakk told Suicide Silence guitarist Chris Garza on his podcast. "You learn how other songs are written, and you're inspired or influenced by them. Or you remember it, and then you tweak it and bend it [to write a song].

"I remember Dime [

Dimebag

Darrell, late

Pantera

guitarist] did this one riff on a certain song," he added. "I go, 'If you didn't tell me that, I would have never got it, because you changed it 'round a bit.' But the spark of inspiration that led you to where you ended up was a specific song.”

The song, written by Ozzy, Zakk and returning bassist Bob Daisley, tore into the televangelist – named 'Jimmy Sinner' – in a sub-four-minute beating.

The second verse,

"Today I saw a miracle man on TV crying, such a hypocritical man, born again, dying,"

refers to the televised meltdown they saw earlier in 1988.

“They were always putting my records down and saying I was the anti-Christ,” Ozzy later told

Uncut

, “and it turned out they weren’t so holy after all.”

The barbs didn't stop there. In the promotional video for the single, which was released a month after the album on October 24, 1988, pokes further fun at the disgraced preacher.

When the music went on, the pigs all took a massive shit at the same time.

Ozzy Osbourne

Filmed in England and directed by Wayne Isham (

Metallica

), the video begins with Ozzy wearing a latex mask which looks like it was moulded from Swaggart's remorseful face.

The performance features Black Sabbath bassist Geezer Butler, who joined the band shortly after the album was recorded, and approximately sixty pigs running amok in a church. The vocalist revealed that the demands of the shoot on his four-legged co-stars led to a ruined pair of suede boots.

“When the music went on, the pigs all took a massive shit at the same time,” Osbourne told

Guitar World

. “Because it was so fucking loud in there. My wife went, ‘Oh, fuck!’ The playback started and they all went

pfffffftttt

! Sixty pigs shitting! I had a pair of brand-new suede boots on, and I never wore them again. I couldn’t get the fucking smell of pig shit out of them.”

Miracle Man

failed to trouble the charts, reaching number 87 on the UK Official Singles Chart. Despite this commercial wobble, the single was a standout track on

No Rest for the Wicked

, which was later certified double platinum.

Swaggart, who died three weeks before Ozzy in 2025, was caught in California, with another sex worker in 1991.

"Now Jimmy, he got busted with his pants down..."
