pending_news.title: How Pearl Jam's intense, combative second album Vs. saved the band's soul
pending_news.rss_body:
In the summer of 1993

Time

magazine approached the management companies looking after

Nirvana

and

Pearl Jam

with a proposal to put their artists on the cover of an autumn issue.

The magazine was keen to do a feature on the rise of ‘grunge’, the underground musical movement that exploded into the national consciousness from the moment, on January 11, 1992, that Nirvana’s

Nevermind

album toppled Michael Jackson’s

Dangerous

from the top of the US

Billboard

chart.

One week earlier, Pearl Jam had scored a minor chart success of their own, when their debut album

Ten

debuted on the

Billboard

200 album chart at Number 155. This was hardly an achievement to warrant the popping of champagne corks, but it was nonetheless a significant moment for the Seattle band, demonstrating that four months on from its August 27, 1991 release,

Ten

still had legs. A further four months later,

Ten

passed the one million sales mark in America.

Then, in August 1992, MTV put Mark Pellington’s haunting video for

Jeremy

– based on the true story of 15-year-old Texan schoolboy Jeremy Wade Delle, who shot himself in front of his teacher and classmates – into rotation. At which point

Ten

began to sell at a rate out-stripping even

Nevermind

.

Mobbed whenever they appeared in public – “You couldn’t go anywhere without causing a scene,” recalled bassist Jeff Ament – the young musicians began to fret as to where their spontaneous, unselfconscious debut album might ultimately lead them. In a bid to slow down their dizzying ascent, Pearl Jam refused to let Epic release the ballad

Black

as a single, and asked for a time-out – no more interviews, no more photo shoots, no more videos. But the record's momentum could not be halted.

“When our record started to sell too, it was weird, and really stressful,” guitarist Stone Gossard told this writer. “Everybody was insecure and tense, it was such an odd time.

“For me personally the stress came from being huge but feeling like you were kinda crap. We couldn’t live up to the bands that we thought were the greatest. I don’t ever remember any thoughts like, ‘Wow, we’ve just made the best album ever.’ I just remember thinking that I was looking forward to making our next one.”

“We didn’t expect the record to be a huge deal,” Jeff Ament added. “But I guess it kinda became one.”

The release of new albums by both Pearl Jam and Nirvana in October 1993 certainly promised to be a huge deal. Though the two bands were often portrayed as bitter rivals in the media – a situation undoubtedly fuelled by snarky Kurt Cobain comments about what he perceived as Pearl Jam’s lack of punk rock credibility – the camps had recently been reconciled, with Cobain and Pearl Jam frontman Vedder even slow-dancing arm-in-arm at the 1992 MTV Awards:

“I probably could have agreed with some of the things he said," Vedder later conceded

.

“The only thing that bothered me about that [alleged rivalry] was because it was public, and people were reacting to it: it wasn’t like between us. There was a certain writer who pulled a quote of Jeff Ament’s out, and pulled a quote of Kurt’s out, and that made for interesting press. But really, I always felt like it us against the world, our town against the world, not our band against another band.”

And so, when they were approached by

Time

, the two groups took a bilateral decision not to participate in the magazine feature. Despite this, when the October 25, 1993 issue of

Time

hit news stands, it was Eddie Vedder’s face staring out from the cover, which hailed “angry young rockers like Pearl Jam” giving voice to “the passions and fears of a generation.”

“We’ve been swallowed up by the mainstream,” Vedder lamented. “No-one is going to want to listen to us.”

For once, Pearl Jam's thoughtful frontman called this wrong.

(Image credit: Time magazine)

Pre-production for the band’s second album began in February 1993 in Seattle, switching to California the following month. Eighteen months on the road had solidified a unit which had only been in existence for six months when they recorded

Ten

, and the new songs largely developed from rehearsal room jams.

The sound was rawer, looser and more in-your-face, exactly what band leader Gossard - who considered

Ten

“over-thought, over-played and over-rocked” - wanted. Working with producer Brendan O’Brien for the first time, the quintet determined to capture this new-found aggression on the record.

With

Vs

. they achieved this and more.

From the opening riff of

Go

, the album has a ferocity and bite which leaves the more stately

Ten

in the dust, sounding like the work of a hardcore punk band rather than a classic rock outfit. On

Animal

Vedder established the idea of the quintet as a unit (“

five against one

”) and expressed his growing revulsion with disingenuous media attempts to co-opt his band’s aesthetic and ideas (“

I’d rather be with an animal

”)

There’s little let-up on this initial explosion of anger. The seething

Daughter

deals with child abuse,

Glorified G

attacks macho gun culture,

W.M.A.

is a scathing dissection of institutionalised racism and police brutality, while the more tender and melodic

Elderly Woman Behind The Counter In A Small Town

was a meditation upon feelings of entrapment and suffocation, which could be read as a metaphor for the band’s own sense of powerlessness as the machine around them grew.

That same notion was made even more explicit on

Leash

, with Vedder singing “

We will find a way, we will find our place

” then screaming “

Get outta my fuckin’ face

.”

“

I will stare the sun down until my eyes go blind

,” Vedder adds defiantly on closing track

Indifference

. “

I won’t change direction, and I won’t change my mind

.”

Lest anyone was still in any doubt, the title of the album too was a challenge, a declaration of independence and intent from a group hell-bent on self-determination, stubbornly refusing to buy into the game.

"For me, that title represented a lot of struggles that you go through trying to make a record," Gossard told

Rolling Stone

. "Your own independence - your own soul - versus everybody else's. In this band, and I think in rock in general the art of compromise is almost as important as the art of individual expression. You might have five great artists in the band, but if they can't compromise and work together, you don't have a great band... When I heard that lyric, it made a lot of sense to me."

The group refused to make a single video for the album, and interviews to promote it were vanishingly rare.

On the surface this stance didn’t immediately impact upon the band’s popularity - the week after

Time

magazine’s ‘grunge’ special was published,

Vs.

, entered the Billboard chart at number 1, selling some 950, 378 copies in its first five days on sale, a sales record that would not be topped for five years.

But in wilfully taking a stand against the commercial forces of MTV, the mass media and, indeed, their own record label’s marketing plans, Pearl Jam would ultimately save their souls and ensure their continued relevance as a band.

An upraised middle finger of a record,

Vs.

still sounds as fierce and visceral today.

pending_news.title: Linkin Park's Emily Armstrong reveals anxieties she held around joining the band
pending_news.rss_body:
Linkin Park

singer Emily Armstrong has discussed what sounds like a classic case of imposter syndrome when it came to taking over vocal duties in Linkin Park. Armstrong was revealed as the band's new frontperson in September 2024 following years of Linkin Park inactivity after the death of

Chester Bennington

seven years earlier, and she reveals that she had periods of intense doubt over whether she was up to the task of replacing one of rock's most celebrated vocalists.

Discussing new Linkin Park documentary

Unshatter

, which delves into Linkin Park's emotional and unlikely comeback, Emily tells

People

:

“You see it in the documentary where I’m just like, ‘Am I even cut out for this?’ You’re trying to give yourself every reason to just be like, ‘You’re not good. Everybody knows these songs.’ ”

On how she overcame her self-doubt, Emily says it was important to remember, "don’t try to be like anybody. You’re not a replacement. Nobody could ever, ever replace Chester. Do what you do.

“The only thing that I could possibly try with the old songs is just to have the same emotional impact as much as I possibly can with the songs, because that’s what you’re ultimately going to want at this point,” she explains. “That’s what I would want as a listener, as a Linkin Park fan. I would want that emotional feeling. And I was like, ‘Okay. I think I could do that.’ ”

Emily's arrival in Linkin Park has proven to be a resounding success; comeback album

From Zero

, released in 2024, was widely praised, and the band have headlined arenas, stadiums and festivals around the world in the years since, including a warmly received headline set at this year's Download Festival in june.

pending_news.title: DEEN CASTRONOVO вернулся на сцену после проблем со здоровьем во время концерта JOURNEY
pending_news.rss_body:
Барабанщик JOURNEY Deen Castronovo вернулся на сцену в субботу вечером (10 октября) и отыграл полноценный концерт вместе с коллегами в Frost Bank Center в Сан-Антонио, штат Техас, всего через два дня после того, как ему стало плохо во время выступления JOURNEY в Талсе, штат Оклахома.

«Он порвал сцену вчера вечером», — написал гитарист JOURNEY Neal Schon в комментарии на своей странице в Йоплобук ранним утром в воскресенье, отвечая на вопрос фаната о том, как Castronovo сыграл в Сан-Антонио. В посте на X Schon добавил: «Deen вернулся в редкостной форме».

По данным Setlist.fm, на концерте в Сан-Антонио Deen исполнил lead-вокал в трёх песнях — «Lights», «Keep On Runnin’» и «Precious Time», — а также разделил ведущий вокал с клавишником Jonathan'ом Cain'ом в «Just The Same Way» и «Anytime».

Перед субботним концертом Castronovo написал на своей странице:

«Спасибо вам всем за невероятную любовь, участие, добрые пожелания, сообщения и смс за последние пару дней. Я не смог ответить каждому лично, но знайте, как много для меня значат ваша доброта и поддержка.

Талса, мне очень жаль, что я не смог доиграть шоу вместе с вами.

Спасибо Jonathan'у Cain'у, Neal'у Schon'у и всем сотрудникам BOK Center за то, что в тот вечер вы молились за меня. Когда я узнал об этом, это глубоко тронуло моё сердце.

Сегодня вечером я выйду на сцену с JOURNEY в Сан-Антонио. С огромной любовью ко всем вам!»

В пятницу Schon пообещал поклонникам JOURNEY, что Castronovo вернётся к концерту в Сан-Антонио.

«Deen чувствует себя отлично, — написал тогда гитарист. — Приходите и помогите нам тепло встретить его после возвращения! Ваши молитвы действительно сработали».

Как сообщается, на концерте в Талсе JOURNEY прервали шоу уже после двух песен: остальные участники покинули сцену, а Cain обратился к залу.

«Посмотрим, как будут развиваться события, — сказал Cain. — Ситуация неприятная. Нам очень жаль. Мы надеемся, что это лишь задержка, но, пожалуйста... простите. Не волнуйтесь. Держите наготове свои молитвы. Держите наготове молитвы за Deen'а Castronovo, все вместе. Спасибо».

Примерно через 10 минут Schon вернулся на сцену и сообщил, что Castronovo доставили в больницу. После этого концерт продолжился, а за установку сел барабанный техник Castronovo Steve Toomey.

pending_news.title: Q&A: New Jersey Death-Thrash Legends Revenant Resurrected
pending_news.rss_body:
Revenant

burned bright in the very late ’80s and early ’90s, culminating with a single full-length album,

Prophecies of a Dying World

(1991), via German then-up ‘n’ comer Nuclear Blast. The group’s demos

Beyond the Winds of Sorrow

(1987),

Asphyxiated Time

(1988), and

Demo 1990

(1990) were traded heavily in the underground. Death-thrash was a thing–think Sadus, Ripping Corpse, Atheist, and Hellwitch–but it wasn’t Revenant. They were unto their own. Six-minute songs (“Asphyxiated Time”), labyrinths of riffs (“Degenaration”), and some of the most vicious vox to come out of a human, punched holes in our collective rotted brains.

Revenant didn’t survive long after Nuclear Blast rejected the follow-up material to

Prophecies of a Dying World

. Call it short-sighted, a colossal error, or a shifting of times, though label still issued Rostok Vampires, Mortification, and other detritus like a factory on overdrive. They signed over to Ed Farshtey’s Rage Records for the

Exalted Being

EP (1992), but by that point, the writing was on the wall. The brightest flame, New Jersey’s most aggressive export of the day, was near its end. When the band said its final goodbye in ’94, the members splintered into various directions. Some continued with deathly metals–bassist Tim Scott found solace in HatePlow–while others pursued more secure careers–vocalist Henry Veggian went into academia–to keep life afloat. Revenant resurfaced briefly with the

Overman

EP (2002), self-releasing their change-of-style charge, a decade removed from wildman antics of

Prophecies of a Dying World

.

If there’s a famous saying about keeping quiet or letting silence prevail, it’s lost on Revenant. While original drummer Will Corcoran sadly passed in 2022, the embers of old, the allure of friendship, of clashing steel beams and complex equations was too hard to fully ignore. The New Jerseyans, now spread across the U.S. and Sweden, have reformed. Frontman Henry Veggian couldn’t let what defined his youth end up a memory–or a constant reminder–so he, thanks to Farshtey’s persistence, called up Scott and guitarist Dave Jengo to float the idea. They were in. As was Incantation and former Revenant guitarist John McEntee. Drummer Todd Gukelberger, of Prime Evil fame, was also added to the lineup, as was bassist Dave Neabore, of Mucky Pup and Season of the Dead, to fill in for Scott.

Decibel

sat down on a Sunday afternoon with the reconstituted Revenant to talk history, respect, friendship, and that the newest iteration of the band isn’t nostalgia… it’s a look into the future.

Why does it make sense for Revenant to reappear now?

Henry Veggian

: I was at a Cannibal Corpse show last year, and I was driving home. It was late at night. I was driving home from Charlotte and I just finally admitted to myself that I missed being in a band. I just missed the collaboration, the chemistry. I had been just ignoring that for a long time. I’m in a phase of life where I’m more about saying yes than saying no. So I picked up the phone, called a friend of mine down here, and asked him if he wanted to start jamming. He said yes. Then, about a month later, we [Revenant] got the offer to reunite. I started talking to everybody else in the band, and we all just decided it was finally time to give it a shot. For me at least, it was about embracing the possibility of music and my love for it again, which I was ignoring.

Dave Jengo

: We actually had a couple of offers. And I think Henry had the biggest one that pushed him a little bit further in that direction. Do you want to elaborate on that, Henry? About Ed [Farshtey]?

Veggian

: Dave and I both received offers for reunion shows separately. They happened around the same time. So, that brought Revenant to us—got us talking. At least for me, the one thing that I started to realize was that there was a whole generation of fans who had never heard us play. They know John. They know Tim [Scott], they know Todd [Gukelberger] from Prime Evil, they know Revenant’s music, but they’d never heard it live. Also, at the same Cannibal Corpse and Municipal Waste show, Fulci were opening. I was on the Waste tour bus, and Dave Witte opened the window and said, “Henry, those are the guys in Fulci—say hello!” He introduced us, and we just started speaking in Italian. Dave was like, “Who’s this guy?!” We had a long conversation; the hands are going. Basically, Italian people talking. I turn around, and [Erik] Rutan’s there scratching his head, “What happened to Hank?! How’d he become Italian?!” [

Laughs

]. There weren’t too many Italians—people who could speak the language—in the metal scene back in the day. So, I never spoke Italian around other people. Dave and Tim knew, though. [

Laughs

] Anyway, the Fulci guys knew about Revenant, all about the band. I was like, Wow, that’s pretty amazing. Then, I started thinking about other bands who had reached out to us. That was motivation too, I think. So when Ed, who’s an old friend, reached out, we were like, yeah.

John McEntee

: It’s not easy to escape metal once you start it. He tried. It’s like a tractor beam. Held out for a while, but he couldn’t do it.

Veggian

: Part of it also was like getting together with John [McEntee] and Charlie [Koryn] at their storage space and recording vocals [for “Circle (Eye of Ascension) VII”] for the Incantation record. I got to admit. I left there, and I was like, yeah, I kind of missed doing this. That put the bug back in me, too.

McEntee

: It was just a weird situation because I just happened to move down here [to North Carolina] not knowing, really, not even thinking about Henry living in the ballpark. I know he lived down South. Probably even in North Carolina, but this was all like years ago. I just happened to realize he was local, and I was like, oh well, that’s pretty cool. For the Incantation thing, I just wanted group vocals with a couple of people. I thought, let’s have Hank do it. He’s part of where I came from musically. Jeff [Becerra] from Possessed is also on the record, ’cause he’s one of the legends that inspired me in the first place. It might not mean anything to other people; to me personally, it was an important little nod. I was able to give Hank a dose of metal, and it ended up without me knowing it that had I nudged Hank a little bit without even really trying.

Veggian

: Jengo was still living in California at the time. So, I think Jengo moving back East was also a part of this. It wasn’t just personal stuff that I was feeling. Some pieces had to start coming together—geographically.

McEntee

: I just want to add that through my travels, obviously everyone knows I’m busy as fuck, usually with Incantation touring and stuff. Every once in a while, either some promoter or just some fan or something will bring up Revenant. Or, bring up some version of some old Revenant thing for me to sign. I just knew that there were people interested in [Revenant], and I even had promoters ask if the band was ever going to do anything. I’d always say, “Ah, no, it’s not going to happen.” Well, here we are.

Sometimes the stars align. How did everyone kind of come back into the fold?

McEntee

: Henry’s stubborn. It basically was his decision if he wanted to do it [reform] or not. I don’t think I ever asked him directly if the band would reform. I kind of knew not to even bother with it. In a way, he always made it clear that I shouldn’t even go there. To my surprise, he called me up. I wasn’t really sure what to say, but “Oh, fuck! Somebody’s passed away.” That’s what was in my head.

Henry made me swear over Parker & Otis lunch not to reveal to anyone—not even

Decibel

—that Revenant had reformed. He texted me out of the blue telling me he had something important to tell me, and that it couldn’t be over the phone. Whatever he was going to tell me had to be in person. I thought the worst, of course. It is, but in the best possible way.

Veggian

: [

Laughs

] It’s true. I had to tell someone that wasn’t already in the band.

McEntee

: [

Laughs

] Then, he asks me about Revenant. He says, “You wanna play some music?” I was like, “Of course!” I don’t know if it’s uncomfortable, but I always really let people know the importance of Revenant, about my evolution as a musician. Revenant was super-important to me at that time in my life. It’s something I’m proud of. Not getting the chance to play in Revenant later was a bit of a bummer, though me leaving Revenant gave me the career that I have now. So, it all worked out in a positive way. I get to play in Revenant again with these guys. It’s nostalgic, but it’s not.

Veggian

: Did you know Dave and John were in a band together like in the mid-’80s before Revenant?

Jengo

: I think I was barely driving, might have just been 17 or something like that. We were still working at the mall, weren’t we?

McEntee

: I worked at Record Town. Jengo worked at KB Toys. The stores were right next door to one another. I remember he was a metalhead. I was a metalhead. Back then it was rare to see metalheads. I was into metal. He was into metal. So, I thought, I’ll just talk to him. It was about finding kindred spirits. We eventually formed the band, Hexes. I think we had the band for a year. Then, Jengo went to Parasyte for a bit.

Jengo

: I was in Parasyte with Tim.

McEntee

: I met Tim at Crazy Eddie’s. That was totally coincidental.

OK, let’s get back on track. Why was it important to have as much of the lineup intact, considering Will [Corcoran] had passed?

Veggian

: When Ed approached me, he asked to get Dave and Tim involved. He asked whether they’d do it. Tim had long moved to Sweden. So, there’d be logistical things to take care of. Once I had Dave and Tim onboard, I said to Ed, “Why don’t I go all in and ask John?” I wasn’t playing guitar much anymore, so I needed a player. I’d rather front the band, be the singer. So, I had a couple of options. John asked for Todd to be involved. We had originally asked Brandon Thomas from Ripping Corpse, but he backed out after a bit. He had a new band and had some shoulder issues. So, that’s how Todd came into the fold.

McEntee

: Actually, I think it was Sam Inzerra from Morpheus Descends right after Brandon. Sam brought up Todd. It was like, ding ding! It made total sense. I can’t imagine anyone else but Todd. Of course, Brandon would’ve ruled, but Todd’s our guy. He’s from the same era as us. He was in Prime Evil, the premier thrash band of the day. I was devastated Prime Evil never took off. I remember looking up to Prime Evil when I was in Revenant.

Veggian

: OK, back to your question. We all bring in our unique histories. But we’re not a prisoner of the past. We’re not in this to sound “old.” We’re going to reinvent Revenant’s music. John has never played some of these songs. Todd obviously hasn’t. Dave, Tim, and I played all the music. So, the new guys are new parts of an old machine. The most important thing with this reunion is that we come to this with fresh ears. So, I’m really happy to have John, Dave, Tim, and Todd in the band. We talk a lot in text and email. The chemistry is real.

Tim Scott

: Well, I’m in Sweden, the most far-flung of the members. I’m learning the songs here and there, playing along to the CDs. The songs are sitting in my backbone. I remember most of the riffs. Mostly correct. [

Laughs

] Dave sent me a video of how he’s playing the songs, so, in a way, we’re jamming online. But I plan on coming to the States soon to get the vibe going again with Dave.

Photo courtesy Henry Veggian

No reservations, Tim? You could’ve said no.

Scott

: I could have said no, but that wasn’t an option. [

Laughs

] In ’94, when we hung it up, I thought I’d never do this [Revenant] again. I moved down to Florida, lost contact with the guys. I’ve always been a bit of a pain. But I’ve always been nostalgic for Revenant. It was a huge part of my life. So, this is really cool that we’re getting together.

Veggian

: After John, Tim’s the most active guy in metal. He was in HatePlow. He’s got Methane in Sweden. Dave Neabore, who’s been filling in and helping us rehearse, has been great. He’s in Mucky Pup and Season of the Dead. So, the only person who’s not been into this the whole time is me!

McEntee

: [To Scott] It’s a long ride to practice. [

Laughs

]

Todd Gukelberger

: I’m just thrilled to have the opportunity to play with these guys because we were all in the same scene together. There was real camaraderie amongst bands and everything back then. When Sam got in touch with me and said, “Hey, you know. Revenant’s getting back together,” I could only say yes.

So, it’s friends first, and everything else second?

Veggian

: Yes, definitely. If it doesn’t work out or whatever, we all tried and we had a good time doing it. For a minute, I thought I had joined Manowar, John, instead of Revenant. I was going to dig out my old cod piece.

McEntee

: We need to be shirtless, Henry. Manowar don’t have shirts. No shirts and furry boots. [

Laughs

]

Veggian

: Oh man. We’re tribal elders now. More gray. I don’t think anyone wants to see us shirtless. [

Laughs

] Anyway, what we’ve done so far—which is to bring us together—has been amazing. We’ve all kind of been through the wringer, to put it mildly. I spent the last 25 years in academia, but I didn’t really ever leave [metal]. I’ve always been going to shows, singing on records. Doing stuff in the background. I have notebooks full of lyrics. I’m always thinking about songs. There’s a sense of unity with Revenant now. I’m loyal to the people and the music. Here’s the thing: Revenant never had an acrimonious split. Every single member of the band that’s played in Revenant is still friends. I still talk to John [Pratscher], our original bass player.

What were the first rehearsals like?

Jengo

: Standing in that room together, with instruments in hand, getting ready to turn on the amps and start playing. What was that like? It felt just like old times, really. I mean, it was, it felt normal and natural. I was excited. I was so pumped to have this happen.

Veggian

: I intentionally stood near Dave while we were playing and rehearsing the first time. Because when we used to rehearse, he was always to my right. I moved the microphone so that I could be facing him, and I could see him off to the side. He was in the corner of my field of vision, and that was familiar to me. Then, I’m looking at Todd, too, thinking, “OK, this is new.” It was weird. It was uncanny. It was familiar and unfamiliar at the same time. And I have to say, when we first kicked into “The Masks of God,” we’d all been practicing it separately, and we almost got through the entire song the first time we tried to play it. And when that happened, in my mind, I thought, “When we get Tim in here, and we get John in here, this is going to sound like a huge giant stomping over the planet.”

McEntee

: It sounded so good.

Jengo

: Not to mention, we were in a nice studio, too. Not my mother’s basement, all cramped in there. [

Laughs

]

Gukelberger

: I thought it was awesome. I really felt like we could do this, that this was going to happen because there was definitely some chemistry between us.

Veggian

: My commitment is all about making it as big as possible in terms of the soundscape that we created in the studio that first time, Chris. It was an awesome feeling. It’s just going to keep getting better as more pieces come together.

So, it wasn’t like when you were 18 and had the worst equipment?

Gukelberger

: [

Laughs

] Oh, no. I brought all kinds of equipment. I had a monitor so I could hear everybody. I didn’t know what was going to be in the room there, but it was a really nice room. We did some cool stuff, though. We flipped the beat around in “Unearthly.” We’re open to suggestions and making improvements. We have the wisdom of time. We’ve played a lot of metal since 1991.

Jengo

: Hopefully, when we get together, it just collides and joins together properly every time. I think that’s more about doing your homework. Come to rehearsal, show up, and be prepared.

Gukelberger

: As long as everybody does that, we’ll be OK. [

Laughs

]

What was the first song the band rehearsed?

Veggian

: It was “Mask of God” from the

Overman

EP, which is a big, kind of heavy song. I remember when I was writing it back in the ’90s, I was going for something like Sepultura’s “Nomad.” That kind of lumbering sludge. It’s got a lot of space in it, unlike the other Revenant songs. To this day, one of my favorite songs of all time is “The Dawn of Megiddo.” I know most of what I wrote back in the day wasn’t that style, but there’s power in Celtic Frost. John’s into them, I think. [

Laughs

] Oh, speaking of John, we’re playing “Asphyxiated Time,” which was a song he was a part of when he was in Revenant early on. Dave and Tim were in the band, too. I’ve asked John to straighten out “Degeneration,” a song Incantation has covered. So, we’re covering all eras of the band and bringing, as Todd said, years of experience and wisdom. We’re tweaking things. We’ve always been tinkerers. That’s why Revenant songs are 6-7 minutes long. Dave would probably identify with this analogy. We’re putting the old motorcycle back together with some new parts.

Tell me about the reissues that are coming out.

Veggian

: Todd helped with the transfer of some of the older demos. There are three reissue goals over the next few years. The first one is going to be the reissue of the collected demos, but as a complete set. There’s an unreleased Revenant demo from 1986 that is all instrumental—no one has ever heard it. I have the only copy. It was the original lineup: me, John, and a guy named Mike [McNeice], who played drums for us briefly and also played in Regurgitation on the first Regurgitation demo. That’s going to be included. Then, it’ll be all of the EPs and demos from the ’90s with Tim and Dave. And we were sitting on an unreleased demo of a song called “The New Paganism,” and that’s been remastered. That will be included too. So, this first reissue is going to be the complete Revenant demos from 1986 to 1994 with some previously unreleased music on it. The last time we did

The Burning Ground

, fans complained that it wasn’t the complete early demos with John. Part of that was just that the source material that I had wasn’t good. I had to find some older boxes and dig through them and get better-quality tapes, and Todd was part of that process in transferring those. We want to reissue

Prophecies

. We have the master tapes. They’re in our possession. We don’t have a plan for that just yet. Then, the other item is the

Overman

EP, which we released as a four-song CD, but there were actually two incomplete songs on there that we could actually go back in and finish and make it like a six-song EP if we wanted to do that. At least one label wants in on the reissues, but we’re not in a hurry because we’ve got a lot of moving parts here. It’s a new era. Tim’s been helping out getting the band online with digital stuff. But let me say this: we’re going to reissue this stuff, but I think the goal here isn’t to just go back and redo all the old stuff. We’re also open to whatever the future might bring. Dave has talked about his desire to write songs. As I said, I have a stack of notebooks of lyrics and stuff. We’re all creative guys.

Jengo

: It’s camaraderie first, you know, and then figuring out what the business element of it is, meaning the releases and labels and all that fun stuff later.

Photo by Chris Bade

So, reissues and then live shows, or the other way around?

Veggian

: Ed’s festival [Rage of Armageddon] is first. And about that festival, I made specific requests to the promoter to get some younger bands I admire on the bill because I wanted to play with them, not in any weird, patronizing way. I wanted to have what John and Todd were saying earlier. The old scene was about bands getting along and being friends, like Prime Evil, Revenant, Incantation, Immolation, Ripping Corpse, and Suffocation. We all used to hang out and play shows together back in the day. It was a community of people. And I’m really excited to be part of that community again as a performing musician. And part of that means learning what’s out there with newer, younger bands.

McEntee

: At the same time, we’re going to have some familiar faces at that show because the Ripping Corpse/Dim Mak guys are in a new band called Temple of Bones, and they’re going to play with us.

Veggian

: Raven, I mean, come on.

Why is the Rage of Armageddon festival special to Revenant?

McEntee

: It’s in Brooklyn. Ed’s one of us, from back in the day. When any of our bands needed help, he was the dude. He still is the dude. I knew that the Revenant thing was going in the right direction, so giving it to Ed, the first show, felt like the right thing to do. He would push us, too. It’s easy for a band to go with the biggest, highest-paying thing, but doing it the proper way is giving it to somebody who was there with us and was a part of the whole community of metal back then, like what I try to do with my fest [Carolina Chainsaw Massacre].

Veggian

: Like John said, Ed was from the old school. He loves the music. He does everything for the music. He’s not a for-profit kind of guy. That’s not his motivation. He’s genuine, and I appreciate that.

Scott

: It’s not a weird thing. Ed will do anything for the bands he believes in. He even took my little shitty thrash metal band out to Brooklyn once, booked us a couple of times, and got us on his

Record of Armageddon

compilation.

McEntee

: That’s true. He supports the underground. He did a lot for the first seven-inch for Revenant back in the day. No, wait, that was the second seven-inch,

Exalted Being

[Rage Records].

Veggian

: Ed was there for us when we had our falling out with Nuclear Blast. He said, “Hey, Nuclear Blast didn’t like that demo. Give it to me, and I’ll put it on my label.” We were labelmates with Prime Evil. Finally!

OK, so, let’s end this thing. Tell me again, who’s putting out the demo reissue and when is the next Rage of Armageddon?

Veggian

: Xtreem, the same label that put out

The Burning Ground

, will get the demos. Not sure about

Prophecies

. We have offers. The other release is still too far out to think about, I think. The next Rage of Armageddon is August of next year. We’d better see you there, Chris!

Revisit

Revenant

on Facebook and

YouTube

. Visit

Methane

on Facebook. Visit

Incantation

on Facebook. Visit

Rage of Armageddon festival

on Facebook.

“Returned to my silent grave

Mute witness to our end

An oath it is that I now sing

The harmony of my suffering

I speak to those who shall forever be” – “Prophecy of a Dying World”

pending_news.title: Tuomas Holopainen reflects on 30 years of Nightwish
pending_news.rss_body:
On October 15, 2026 it was announced that Nightwish had

parted ways with vocalist Floor Jansen

after 13 years. In statements released by both Floor and the group, they described the split as "a mutual decision". At the time of writing, both parties and unavailable for comment.

Earlier this summer Hammer flew out to Finland to spend time with founder Tuomas Holopainen in the band's birthplace of Kitee to discuss 30 years of Nightwish history and what the future might look like.

On June 16, 2023,

Nightwish

played the best gig of their lives. That’s how founder and keyboardist

Tuomas Holopainen

sees it, anyway. Looking out at a sold-out crowd at Kitee’s Rantakenttä baseball stadium, he recognised more faces than usual – friends, cousins, siblings, fans who’d travelled across the world. This was the first time Nightwish had played in their hometown in almost 20 years and, for Tuomas, it felt like he’d come full circle.

“When we got onstage, I could almost see the studio building where we’d recorded our very first demo,” he says now. “I remembered being there almost 30 years before, now I’m playing to 11,000 people. I still get shivers just thinking about it. What a journey!”

Several songs from the Kitee gig appear on a new live compilation,

The Greatest 30 Years On Earth

, released in December to coincide with Nightwish’s 30th anniversary. Since forming in this small rural town in 1996, the band have risen to become their country’s biggest musical export and one of the defining groups of the 21st century, doing more than anyone to shape the modern

symphonic metal

movement.

Despite everything he’s achieved, Tuomas still lives here in Kitee. He isn’t just its most famous son, he’s its biggest cheerleader. So much so that he’s agreed to give

Hammer

a tour of his birthplace. It’s clear that Tuomas Holopainen loves Kitee. And Kitee loves Tuomas Holopainen back.

“What brings you here?” asks the taxi driver who collects us from the local train station. We’re here to write a piece about Nightwish, we explain.

“Ah, you’ll be seeing Tuomas then,” she says. “Tell him I said hello.”

“I know her,” Tuomas says with a chuckle, when we meet him for our tour the next day. “I mean, there’s, like, three taxi drivers out here. It’s a small town.”

To understand just how remarkable Nightwish’s rise has been, you first have to understand just how remote Kitee is. A four-hour-plus train ride away from Helsinki, civilisation drops away and we’re treated to the sights of Finland’s rugged wilderness. Trees. Trees. More trees. A lake. More trees.

There’s something about being on an island – you can’t just walk away

Tuomas Holopainen

With a population of fewer than 10,000 and one main road, Kitee is more like a glorified waystation than a town in the traditional sense. But Tuomas insists he’s never been tempted to up sticks for the bright lights of the big city.

“Never,” he says proudly. “I’ve always been a country boy. I just love this town because I know everybody and everybody knows me, so I get this peace and solitude. It’s a safe haven.”

It’s appropriate that he’s acting as our tour guide today. One of his first jobs as a teenager was showing people around the local Lutheran church. His grandfather served as pastor there before Tuomas was born, and the Nightwish man can trace his mother’s family line back to 16th-century religious reformist Martin Luther himself. The young Tuomas preferred fantasy novels and movies to scripture, and he still holds the fantastical close to his heart today. The otherwise unassuming car he picks us up in for our tour of the town is nicknamed ‘Gryffindor’. “The licence plate says ‘GRF’,” he says sheepishly, adding that there’s a large Harry Potter flag in the boot.

Encouraged into music by his mother, he learned piano and later played clarinet and the saxophone in his school’s classical and jazz groups. It was there that he met future Nightwish guitarist Emppu Vuorinen and singer Tarja Turunen. On July 6, 1996, when he was 19, Tuomas invited the pair to his parents’ cabin on an island in nearby Lake Pyhäjärvi to create a new band. Sitting around a campfire, he shared songs he’d written while doing his national service in the Finnish army. It was the moment Nightwish were born.

“In the guestbook, you can find the inscription saying that a band had formed that day,” Tuomas says. “It doesn’t say ‘Nightwish’, but it says we were there.”

He bought the island home from his parents a few years ago, and goes there a few times a year to write lyrics.

“There’s no electricity or running water, it’s very primal,” he says. “That’s why I like it. It’s very solitary and peaceful. There’s something about being on an island – you can’t just walk away.”

(Image credit: John McMurtrie)

Kitee was once the moonshine capital of Finland, famous for its illicit hooch. Today, one of its biggest attractions is the permanent Nightwish exhibition, opened in 2020 to celebrate the band. Inside sits 30 years’ worth of memorabilia. The exhibition doesn’t just tell the story of the band, it charts Tuomas’s own journey too.

In one room, we spot a photo showing him with neat short hair and a crisp white shirt, looking every inch the nerdy schoolboy. This was before he took a destiny-changing student exchange trip to the US, where he was taken to a Metallica gig. Soon after returning to Finland, he joined local goth/doom band Dismal Silence.

Before our first show, I thought I was going to die

Tuomas Holopainen

“I loved it immediately,” he says. “Being with your mates, playing every night and arranging your own songs. That all happened in the fall of 1993. Ever since, I’ve been in bands: Dismal Silence, then Darkwoods My Betrothed, Nattvindens Gråt and then Nightwish.”

Nattvindens Gråt gave Tuomas his first experience of touring, when they supported Dutch goth-metal band Wish in the summer of 1996.

“We played in Hamburg and there was literally one guy there,” says Tuomas. “He left after two songs. We did 10 shows in 10 days, and the biggest attendance at any of those shows was 70 people.”

Just up the road from the Nightwish exhibition, and directly opposite the baseball stadium, sits the studio where Nightwish recorded their first four albums. It also served as a hangout for Tuomas and his friends, and anyone else who wanted to come along.

“The amount of cigarettes and booze consumed here must be astronomical,” he says.

The studio was also where Nightwish played their first ever show, on New Year’s Eve 1997. Their debut album,

Angels Fall First

, had been released a couple of months earlier and reached No.5 in the Finnish charts. After being offered the chance to go on tour, the band decided to test the water with a hometown show.

“I was so scared I thought I was going to die,” Tuomas admits. “I think I vomited before the show. I’d played shows before, but I was just the keyboardist in those bands, I wasn’t responsible for those songs. Nightwish was my baby, I was like, ‘I can’t fucking do this!’”

As it turned out, they could. Playing for 30 minutes in front of 250 people, the band had a blast.

“We got so drunk that none of us made it home,” Tuomas recalls. “We all slept on the floor side-by-side.”

(Image credit: Press/Nuclear Blast)

In early 1998, the band went out on their first full tour, playing with fellow Finns Children Of Bodom. “We clicked immediately,” Tuomas recalls. “I became friends with Alexi [Laiho, late CoB frontman] right away. Four years later we went to Disneyland Florida with him. We were just two kids who loved the same things – music and Disney theme parks. We were close right up until he died.”

The success of

Angels Fall First

made it clear to Tuomas that it was decision time for Nightwish: they had to dedicate everything to the band or risk it falling apart.

“I spoke to Tarja and Emppu about what ambitions they had,” he recalls. “It was like, ‘Let’s see how this goes for a few years. See how far we can get.’ We got pretty far.”

The band’s second album, 1998’s

Oceanborn

, was another step up. The track

Sacrament Of Wilderness

gave the band their first No.1 single in Finland. Tuomas had taken a job as a supply teacher, and was at work when he found out it had topped the charts.

“I was calling everybody else up to share the news,” he says. “It was up against Madonna and Guns N’ Roses!”

The band got their first No.1 album with 2000’s

Wishmaster

. The same year, they ill-advisedly took part in a competition to become Finland’s entry in the international cheese-fest the Eurovision Song Contest, coming third (“Entirely my idea, everyone else was against it,” concedes Tuomas). More successful was their very first tour of Latin America.

“The response was like we were the Rolling Stones,” Tuomas says. “It felt great to see people going crazy over stuff I’d created in my parents’ house.”

When Tuomas was young, he used to play baseball at Rantakenttä. He still loves the sport, but admits he had to hang up his mitt because he “wasn’t a team player”. When we point out there are at least a couple of people who’ve left Nightwish’s ranks who might agree, he laughs it off.

For all the successes the band have enjoyed, things haven’t always been sunny. In 2001, just as they were picking up serious steam, tensions rose with then-bassist Sami Vänskä to the point where Tuomas seriously considered ending the band altogether.

“Sami’s heart just wasn’t in it anymore,” Tuomas says. “We’re still friends now and there’s no bad blood, but we realised that to stay friends he needed to leave. Then Marko [Hietala, bassist and co-vocalist] joined, of course.”

Four years later, there was even more turbulence. The band’s 2004 album,

Once

, had kicked things to another level for them, not least in the UK and America. But problems were brewing with Tarja Turunen.

“I loved the first half of the Once [Upon A] Tour,” Tuomas says. “Then all hell broke loose in 2005, which was the darkest period of the band.”

He’s referring, of course, to the night of October 21, 2005, when, immediately after the final show of the Once Upon A Tour in Helsinki, the band delivered a letter to Tarja accusing her of putting her solo career above Nightwish and telling her she was fired from the band. After the letter was published online, an ugly media storm broke out. Even the country’s then-Prime Minister was asked to comment on the split in Parliament.

“We get blamed for what happened, for good reason,” says Tuomas. “But there was no future for us together. We were just operating in survival mode and plagued by these dark thoughts. We got completely butchered in the media – it was like we were these evil neanderthals who’d hurt our wonderful ex-singer. I got some really interesting letters, let’s put it that way.”

Tarja and Tuomas have exchanged a few emails in recent years, but Tuomas says that’s as close as they’re likely to get to repairing their relationship.

“It was a divorce, and an ugly one at that, so I think we have our own lives now,” he says. “Someone did say to me if we got Tarja and Marko [Hietala, who left in 2020] back in, we could tour just South America for a year straight. That’s not gonna happen.”

After Tarja’s dismissal, Nightwish found a replacement in Anette Olzon, who joined the band in May 2007. According to Tuomas, she was one of 2,200 candidates who applied for the job.

“We’d already recorded [the music for] the album [2007’s Dark Passion Play], so it was a bit like, ‘The deadline is approaching,’” he says. “None of the 2,200 candidates was immediately spot-on, but Anette was the best of what we had. Her voice was so refreshing to all of us, we loved her interpretations of the songs.”

The split with Tarja didn’t halt Nightwish’s rise.

Dark Passion Play

and 2011’s

Imaginaerum

continued their hot streak, with the latter giving them their first US Top 30 album. Memorably, they played in China for the first time in 2008. Tuomas says the authorities banned them from throwing plectrums into the audience in case fans stood up during the show.

But more upheaval came in 2012 when Anette left the band in controversial circumstances midway through a US tour. She had publicly voiced her displeasure at being temporarily replaced by Arch Enemy’s Alissa White-Gluz and Elize Ryd of Amaranthe at a gig in Denver when she was too ill to perform. Anette subsequently contested that she’d been fired because she was pregnant and could not tour extensively – something the band denied.

Tuomas won’t go into specifics today, but does hint at some regrets about the period.

“It’s so easy to think, ‘We must strike while the iron is hot’, but you have to know your limits,” Tuomas says now. “When Anette joined the band, we started the Dark Passion Play tour, which lasted for two years and 250 shows. We did four American tours on that record alone, just constant touring, and the result is what it was. A silly thing to do.”

John McMurtrie

John McMurtrie

John McMurtrie

John McMurtrie

John McMurtrie

We stop for lunch at a local pizzeria, where we’re greeted by a massive portrait of the band from the Once era. With his long dark hair and gothic clothes, the Tuomas in the painting looks like he’s trying to be Peter Steele.

“Back then I was obsessed with darkness,” he says, looking at the picture with mild embarrassment. “I grew out of it, I’ve changed a lot, personality-wise.”

Certainly, the last decade or so seems to have been more stable for Nightwish, at least when it comes to singers. Former After Forever singer Floor Jansen replaced Anette Olzon as interim vocalist for the remaining dates on the Imaginaerum tour, before joining as a full-time member in 2013.

If we’d continued as we were, people were gonna die

Tuomas Holopainen

The eventual departure of longtime drummer Jukka Nevalainen in 2019 after stepping away from touring five years earlier was amicable (he would ultimately be replaced by Kai Hahto). But Nightwish’s world was rocked once more in the midst of the pandemic, when Marko Hietala dropped a bombshell and announced that he was leaving, citing mental health issues.

“I was gutted,” Tuomas says. “We all knew he’d got his problems with depression. But he called me in December [2020] just saying, ‘I can’t do this anymore. I’m too sick – I need to do something else.’ My initial reaction was laughter – surely it wasn’t happening again. I called Emppu, and he said, ‘Maybe we should quit.’ I agreed.”

However, getting new bassist Jukka Koskinen onboard was a turning point. “Sure enough, everything worked. The sun started to shine again. That’s what this band does: it keeps surviving,” he says, adding that he and Marko are still on good terms.

Even then, the drama wasn’t over. Floor Jansen was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2022 (her treatment was, thankfully, successful). The following year, a shock announcement that the band wouldn’t be touring “for the foreseeable future” set alarm bells ringing among fans.

As we speak, that memorable hometown show at Kitee’s baseball stadium was their last-but-one gig. Reflecting on the decision today, Tuomas insists that it was critical to the band’s survival – he was burned out and concerned about his wellbeing.

“I reached a point where I felt that I couldn’t do it anymore,” he explains. “There’s so much shit that goes on when you’re on tour and I’m slightly traumatised. I told the band they could go on without me, but they wouldn’t have it. Other members of the band said, ‘No, we need a break.’ If we’d continued as we were, people were gonna die.”

Being off the road hasn’t hurt their career. 2024’s

Yesterwynde

continued their chart-topping streak in Finland and gave them their second UK Top 20 album following 2015’s grandiose

Endless Forms Most Beautiful

.

“Nightwish has always been more than the sum of its parts,” Tuomas says bullishly. “I honestly think at this point, if any member – including myself – left, the rest of them could continue. Any of us. Because we have evidence enough that this band can work with any combo.”

Tuomas’s home sits a little way out of Kitee itself. From the outside at least, it exudes a very fitting Addams Family vibe, as well as an air of solitude that seems to suit a man who values his privacy. A jetty juts out on the serene water of a lake. Tuomas often relaxes in his sauna before sitting on the jetty to write lyrics and reflect. He’s had plenty of time to do the latter recently.

“That’s why we’re on a break right now,” he says. “We’ve been in the same job for 30 years – we can take a vacation. I love having the time to read, and take a long walk. But I also don’t want to do that for the rest of my life.”

He’s getting itchy feet. In July, he played a few Finnish shows with Auri, the folk project he formed with his wife, Johanna Kurkela, and Nightwish multi-instrumentalist/ co-vocalist Troy Donockley. Tuomas is also working on his second solo album, with plans to record the final parts later this year. After that, he’s planning to properly start work on the next Nightwish album.

“I got my health back, I feel more inspired than ever – proof of that is that I’ve already got six new Nightwish songs done,” he says. “Every time I sit in front of my keyboard, I’m like, ‘Ah yeah this is great! Just wait till everyone hears this.’ It’s exhilarating. Next year is too early to be going back on tour. The year after, possibly? I want to do another album before any live shows, and that’s definitely happening. We’ve already reserved things for that next year.”

The upcoming

The Greatest 30 Years On Earth

compilation is both proof that rumours of Nightwish’s demise have been greatly exaggerated, and a celebration of the ongoing legacy of the band Tuomas formed in this tiny town all those years ago that has defined his life ever since.

“This stuff will live on for 100 years after I’m dead,” he says. “I wouldn’t have met my wife without Nightwish. It’s brought all the best and worst things into my life, but the good far exceeds the bad.”

The 30 Greatest Years On Earth is out December 11 via Nuclear Blast.
